item.title: Maven Robotics Raises $100M Series A for General-Purpose Industrial Robots
item.description: Maven Robotics, a Santa Clara, California-based company building general-purpose robots for industrial work, has raised a $100 million Series A led by RoboStrategy. LocalGlobe, Vine Ventures, and XTX Ventures were among the other investors. The company is led by CEO Hamza Derbas and CFO Khalid De...
item.content:encoded:
Maven Robotics, a Santa Clara, California-based company building general-purpose robots for industrial work, has raised a $100 million Series A led by RoboStrategy. LocalGlobe, Vine Ventures, and XTX Ventures were among the other investors.


The company is led by CEO Hamza Derbas and CFO Khalid Derbas.


A Seasoned Autonomy Team


Hamza Derbas has spent more than two decades developing autonomous systems, with stints at Apple, Tesla, Rivian, Cruise, Zoox, Ford and Archer Aviation. Khalid Derbas brings experience as an investor and operator who has scaled businesses across global markets.


Maven says its broader team has more than 200 years of combined experience in AI, robotics, engineering and autonomy, much of it from programs that shipped hardware at scale.


"Maven has a top-tier team with a track record of shipping high-performing products," said Jack Pearson, principal at RoboStrategy.

Starting With the Pallet


Maven's system integrates hardware, software, and AI into a single robotics platform. Rather than launch with a humanoid or a broad set of tasks, the company is starting with mixed-case palletizing and tote handling, jobs that are repetitive, physically demanding, and hard to staff.


Maven sizes that initial opportunity at $80 billion, and puts the wider market, including complex material handling and assembly, at more than $1 trillion.


The robots are already deployed with a Fortune 250 consumer packaged goods company, and Maven says it is expanding to additional customers. It expects to log more than 100,000 autonomous operating hours by the end of 2026 and is targeting 1 million hours by the end of 2027.


The Vision


"Intelligent industrial robots promise an incredible future," Hamza Derbas said. "If we can activate autonomous labor, we can build a world of infinitely elastic industrial capacity."


Pulse 2.0 reported that the funding will help Maven scale its industrial robots across manufacturing and logistics.


Why It Matters


General-purpose robotics has become one of the hottest categories in venture capital, with investors betting that AI models can make machines adaptable enough to handle many tasks instead of one. Most of that money has gone to humanoid developers still years from broad deployment.


Maven is taking a more practical route: prove the platform on a single high-volume job inside real factories and warehouses, rack up operating hours, then expand. Autonomous hours logged in production are the metric that will show whether that approach can scale.

item.title: Sharrp Ventures Just Bet $1M That Protein Pantry Can Change What’s in Your Pantry
item.description: Protein Pantry, a Delhi-based clean-label frozen food brand, has raised Rs 9 crore — roughly $1 million — in a seed round led by Sharrp Ventures , the family office backing consumer brands out of Mumbai. The round closed less than a year after the company started selling. Who else is in the round...
item.content:encoded:
Protein Pantry, a Delhi-based clean-label frozen food brand, has raised Rs 9 crore — roughly $1 million — in a seed round led by Sharrp Ventures, the family office backing consumer brands out of Mumbai. The round closed less than a year after the company started selling.


Who else is in the round

Peercheque, Consumer Collective by Atrium and Indian Silicon Valley Capital joined the round, alongside an angel list heavy on consumer-brand operators: Mamaearth co-founder Varun Alagh, Rishubh Satiya, Avnish Anand, Arush Chopra, Saurabh Munjal and Signal Ventures, among others.

That investor mix says something about the company's positioning. Protein Pantry is not being sold as a food-science play. It is being sold as a brand bet — the kind that lives or dies on repeat purchase rates and shelf placement.


The product

Founded in November 2025 by Disha Bhattacharya and Prashanth Bhushan, the company makes ready-to-cook, high-protein frozen items for Indian households: soya chaap, kebabs, cutlets, and falafels. The pitch is what they leave out. No refined flour, no preservatives, no palm oil. Everything is baked rather than fried, and the ingredient lists are meant to read like a home kitchen shelf.


It is a narrow lane with real demand behind it. Protein consciousness has moved from gym culture into mainstream Indian grocery baskets over the past few years, and the frozen aisle has been slow to respond with anything that isn't battered and deep-fried.

Where it sells

The brand says it now serves more than 30,000 households, with what it describes as a strong repeat rate. It sells direct-to-consumer and through quick-commerce platforms including Blinkit, FirstClub and Flipkart Minutes, across Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Jaipur.


Quick commerce is the interesting part of that distribution story. For a frozen brand, ten-minute delivery solves the problem that has historically capped the category in India— last-mile cold-chain reliability and the household freezer space needed to justify a bulk trip to a supermarket. Selling through dark stores lets a young brand skip both.


What the money is for

The capital primarily goes toward setting up and scaling a manufacturing unit, with continued spend on R&D and the supply chain. That is the standard next move for a frozen brand that has proven demand on someone else's production line: margins in the category are made or lost in the plant, and co-manufacturing caps both quality control and unit economics.


Owning production also matters for the clean-label claim. Preservative-free frozen food is harder to make consistently than the conventional version, and the failure mode — inconsistent texture, short shelf life, spoilage in transit — is the kind that kills repeat purchase quickly.


The read

A $1 million seed is little money, and Protein Pantry is competing in a category where established players have plant capacity, distribution muscle, and pricing room it does not have yet. It has a clearer product story than most of the frozen aisle and a distribution channel that didn't exist when the incumbents were built. The next twelve months, and whether the manufacturing line comes online on schedule, will show whether that is enough.

item.content:encoded:
Disclosure: YourInfoDaily may earn a commission if you buy through links in this article. Offers change and are often targeted, so confirm the terms in your own account before buying.

Before you buy Rapid Rewards points, know these five things: your discount is personal, a point is worth about 1.3 cents, bought points don't count toward the Companion Pass, the purchase isn't airfare to your card, and point bookings are unusually easy to cancel. Together, they tell you when buying helps and when it doesn't.


1. Your discount is not the same as everyone else's

Southwest's standard price is 3 cents per point. It discounts points regularly, but not equally. One Mile at a Time reported that during a sale running September 2 to October 2, 2026, different members were offered 35%, 45%, or 50% off. Award Travel Finder's tracker, updated October 9, 2026, listed a 50% discount through October 29.

On a purchase of 60,000 points, those tiers look like this:

  • 50% off: $900, or 1.5 cents per point.
  • 45% off: $990, or 1.65 cents per point.
  • 35% off: $1,170, or 1.95 cents per point.

The discount in that sale applied only to purchases of at least 3,000 points in one transaction.


What to do: log in and look at your own offer before you read anyone's verdict on the sale, including this one. A 50% offer and a 35% offer lead to different answers.


2. A point is worth about 1.3 cents, almost every time

With most airlines, a point's value swings widely, and experts hunt for sweet spots. Southwest is different. Frequent Miler explains that award prices depend on demand and the flight's cash price, rising and falling with the fare. Any seat for sale can be booked with points.


The result is predictable value. Frequent Miler's benchmark is 1.3 cents per point. One Mile at a Time estimates 1.1 to 1.5 cents.


That predictability works against buyers. No hidden jackpot makes points bought at 1.5 cents suddenly worth 4 cents. One Mile at a Time concludes that buying at 1.5 cents or more rarely makes sense, because points usually redeem for less.


What to do: treat buying as a way to complete a booking, not as a discount on travel.

3. Bought points do not count toward the Companion Pass

The Companion Pass lets a named companion fly with you for only the taxes. Frequent Miler requires 135,000 qualifying points in a calendar year.


Purchased points do not qualify. Neither do points transferred from another member, most bonus points, or points transferred in from hotel partners or Chase Ultimate Rewards. What does count: base points from paid flights, Southwest credit card spending, card welcome bonuses, and many partner activities.


What to do: if the pass is your target, put your money into paid flights and card spending. Buy points only for redemptions.


See the Rapid Rewards offer on your account.


4. There are limits, and your card sees a different merchant

According to One Mile at a Time, you can buy up to 60,000 points per day, with no annual limit. That is unusually open. Most programs cap purchases annually.

The sale is processed by Points.com, not by Southwest. Your credit card will not record it as an airline purchase, so do not expect an airfare bonus category to apply. One Mile at a Time suggests using a card with a minimum spending requirement or one with strong everyday rewards.


What to do: choose a card for its base earning rate, and buy only what your booking needs. The lack of an annual cap isn't a reason to stock up.


5. Points bookings are easy to undo, and points never expire

This is the best argument for holding Rapid Rewards points at all.

  • Cancellations. Frequent Miler notes that you can cancel award flights for no fee up to 10 minutes before departure, with points returned immediately. One Mile at a Time adds that a canceled cash ticket becomes a travel credit for a future flight, while redeposited points can be used for anyone.
  • Changes. If your flight price drops after you book, Frequent Miler says changing to a cheaper fare returns the difference in points.
  • Expiration. Rapid Rewards points do not expire, and no activity is needed to keep them. Closing your account forfeits them.


What to do: if your travel dates are uncertain, a points booking gives you a clean exit. After you book, check the price again periodically. If it falls, rebook and collect the difference.


Top up your Rapid Rewards balance.


So when should you buy?

  • Buy when you are a few thousand points short of a flight you are ready to book. A 3,000-point top-up at 50% off costs about $45.
  • Consider buying when your plans may change, and you value getting points back more than holding a travel credit.
  • Do not buy to pay for a whole trip at a 35% or 45% discount, to chase the Companion Pass, or because a sale is ending. Another sale will follow.


A quick self-check

  • What discount does my account show?
  • What is the cash fare, and what is the points price?
  • How many points am I actually missing?
  • If I cancel, would I rather hold points or a travel credit?


Two more notes. Southwest offers a Cash + Points option, which Frequent Miler says yields poor value per point. And free checked bags now depend on your fare, elite status, or a Southwest credit card, so include bag costs when you compare a Southwest fare with a competitor's.


FAQ


How much are Rapid Rewards points worth?

About 1.3 cents each by Frequent Miler's benchmark, with a typical range of 1.1 to 1.5 cents.


Is there a limit on how many Southwest points you can buy?

Up to 60,000 per day, with no annual cap.


Do Rapid Rewards points expire?

No.


Can I get a refund on points I buy?

Treat purchases as final and read the terms shown at checkout before you pay.

item.content:encoded:
Manny Larcher is one of several speakers confirmed for OhioXR 2026, taking the stage to discuss where the creator economy is headed, beyond the metrics platforms prefer to showcase.


Billed as Ohio's first cross-industry XR event, the conference brings together voices from healthcare, manufacturing, aerospace, financial services, and education under one roof at the PAST Foundation Innovation Lab in Columbus. Organizers have been explicit about the format: practitioner-led sessions, no pay-to-speak slots, and no vendor pitches dressed up as talks.


Larcher's session will draw on three different vantage points he's built over the past decade. As founder of YourInfoDaily, a media outlet covering music, business, and culture since 2014, he's watched how creator-driven content actually performs and monetizes in the market. Through AuxChord, a live transactional review and feedback marketplace, he's built infrastructure specifically for managing and monetizing live-streaming in real time. And with Colaeb, a human-led business matchmaking platform he's run for six years, he's accumulated research on what makes professional introductions and partnerships actually hold up.


The session will pull those threads together: monetization models that survive algorithm changes, the traits of creator-brand partnerships that last, and where immersive and XR formats fit into the next phase of live content.

item.title: How Much Did VEIR Raise? Inside the $110M Superconducting Round
item.description: VEIR, a Woburn, Massachusetts-based company that makes superconducting power systems, has raised $110 million in an oversubscribed Series C round co-led by Matter Venture Partners and Tyche Partners. New investors LG Technology Ventures, Gates Frontier, Sabanci Climate Ventures and Hui Capital jo...
item.content:encoded:
VEIR, a Woburn, Massachusetts-based company that makes superconducting power systems, has raised $110 million in an oversubscribed Series C round co-led by Matter Venture Partners and Tyche Partners.


New investors LG Technology Ventures, Gates Frontier, Sabanci Climate Ventures and Hui Capital joined, along with existing backers Engine Ventures, Galvanize Climate Solutions, Piva Capital, Congruent Ventures and VXI Capital. The round brings VEIR's total funding to $225 million, following a $75 million Series B in January 2025.


What VEIR Does


Most electricity moves through copper or aluminum, which lose energy as heat and need large amounts of physical space to carry heavy loads. Superconducting cables, cooled to extremely low temperatures, carry electricity with almost no resistance, allowing much more power to move through a much smaller footprint.


VEIR packages superconducting cables with cryogenic cooling, controls, termination units and monitoring into a complete power delivery system. The company says this reduces the space, materials and installation work needed compared with conventional copper systems.


VEIR was founded in 2019 and is led by CEO and co-founder Tim Heidel. It has demonstrated a 3-megawatt system and is working with unnamed customers and partners on reference designs and commercial deployments.


The AI Data Center Focus


VEIR's first commercial target is behind-the-meter power inside AI data centers, meaning power distribution on the operator's side of the utility connection. As AI chips draw more power per rack, operators are running into the physical limits of how much copper they can fit into a building.


Heidel has said AI infrastructure is advancing fast enough that power delivery must be rethought rather than just optimized. Tyche Partners managing partner Weijie Yun has made a similar case, arguing that the physics of copper has become a fundamental limit.


How the Money Will Be Used


According to The AI Insider, VEIR will use the funds to expand manufacturing capacity, advance its product line, build out technical and commercial teams and support its first commercial projects.


Why It Matters


Power has become the main constraint on AI infrastructure. Much of the attention goes to generation and grid connections, but moving power efficiently inside dense data centers is a growing problem of its own. VEIR's raise reflects investor interest in the full power stack behind AI, and its next challenge is proving superconducting systems can be manufactured and installed at commercial scale.

item.title: Vinci Pharmaceuticals Closes $8M Series A for Needle-Free Retinal Drug Implant
item.description: Vinci Pharmaceuticals, a specialty eye care company based in Avon-by-the-Sea, New Jersey, has closed a Series A financing of more than $8 million to advance its EPIPLANT drug delivery platform. Dynagrow Capital led the round, with support from MintPharma Capital. The raise follows $8.5 million in...
item.content:encoded:
Vinci Pharmaceuticals, a specialty eye care company based in Avon-by-the-Sea, New Jersey, has closed a Series A financing of more than $8 million to advance its EPIPLANT drug delivery platform. Dynagrow Capital led the round, with support from MintPharma Capital.


The raise follows $8.5 million in seed financing, bringing Vinci's total funding to more than $16.5 million.


What EPIPLANT Is


Many of the most common treatments for retinal diseases, including those affecting the macula, are delivered by injection directly into the eye, often every month or two. The treatment burden is heavy, and many patients stop treatment early, which can lead to vision loss.


EPIPLANT is designed to avoid that. It is a bioerodible implant placed on the outer surface of the eye, against the sclera, that releases medication to the retinal tissues over time without injections into the eye. The platform can currently deliver small-molecule drugs and is designed to work with a range of active ingredients.


The technology was developed in the lab of retina specialist Karl Csaky, MD, PhD, and is licensed from the Retina Foundation of the Southwest in Dallas. Vinci says it holds multiple granted patents and has completed preliminary preclinical testing.


How the Money Will Be Used


The proceeds will fund manufacturing, testing and release of its lead product, EPIPLANT VCI-002, under good manufacturing practice standards, as well as a planned Phase 1/2a first-in-human clinical trial in 2027.


Co-founder, chairman and CEO Philip A. Gioia described the financing as an important step toward that first human study. Dynagrow Capital managing director Sarah Hassan said a needle-free option could help reduce the high dropout rates caused by the burden of current treatment.


Why It Matters


Retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration and diabetic macular edema are among the leading causes of vision loss, and the drugs used to treat them form one of the largest markets in ophthalmology. Much of the industry's recent innovation has focused on making treatments last longer between injections.


Vinci is aiming further, removing the intraocular injection entirely. The approach still has to show in humans that it can deliver enough drug to the retina safely and consistently. With the Series A closed, the company has funding to manufacture clinical supply and bring EPIPLANT to its first patients.


Source


PR Newswire — "Vinci Pharmaceuticals Inc. Closes More Than $8 Million Series A Financing to Advance EPIPLANT™ Drug Delivery Platform"

item.title: How Much Did Gramiyaa Raise? Inside the $2.1M Series A
item.description: Gramiyaa, a Bengaluru-based cold-pressed cooking oil brand, has raised Rs 18.65 crore, about $2.1 million, in a Series A round led by new investor Optiscape Network Holdings, according to regulatory filings reported by Entrackr. item.content:encoded:
Gramiyaa, a Bengaluru-based cold-pressed cooking oil brand, has raised Rs 18.65 crore, about $2.1 million, in a Series A round led by new investor Optiscape Network Holdings, according to regulatory filings reported by Entrackr.


Optiscape put in Rs 9 crore. Existing investors Homegrown Ventures and Campus Fund invested Rs 4.5 crore and Rs 4 crore, while Sarya Global Holdings and Rasagna Pulapaka contributed smaller amounts. Entrackr estimates Gramiyaa's post-money valuation at about Rs 110 crore, up 49% from Rs 74 crore at its previous round.


What Gramiyaa Sells


Founded in 2016 by Sibi Manivannan, Gramiyaa makes its oils in-house using traditional cold-press methods, which extract oil without high heat or chemical solvents. Its range includes groundnut, coconut, sesame and mustard oils, along with virgin coconut and olive oils.


The brand sells through its own website and a long list of online channels, including Amazon, BigBasket, DMart Ready and FirstClub, as well as quick commerce apps Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart.


The Financials


Gramiyaa's revenue rose 72.7% year over year to Rs 19 crore in FY25. Losses grew about 12.7 times to Rs 4 crore over the same period, reflecting heavier spending on growth. The company has not yet filed its FY26 results.


The new funding follows a Rs 7.2 crore pre-Series A round in March 2025 led by Homegrown Ventures, with Campus Fund and Mumbai Angels participating. After the latest round, Homegrown Ventures is the largest outside shareholder at about 17%. The co-founders, Manivannan, Mohamed Yaseen and Naveenrajaman RL, together hold just over half the company.


According to the filings, the money will be used for growth capital and general corporate purposes.


Why It Matters


Cold-pressed oils have moved from health food stores into the mainstream in India, helped by growing consumer interest in less-processed foods and by quick commerce apps that put niche brands in front of urban shoppers within minutes. That has drawn investors to a crowded field of direct-to-consumer staples brands.


Gramiyaa's numbers show both sides of the model: fast revenue growth through online and quick commerce channels, and rising losses to fund it. The Series A gives the company runway to keep scaling, with the next test being whether it can narrow losses as it grows.

Baobab Ventures, Lanai Ventures, Acurio Ventures and Masia VC invested. The company was co-founded by co-CEO Dani Diestre, Aniol Carreras and Jacob Bamio. WHAT AUTENTIC AI DOES Tradit...
item.content:encoded:
Autentic AI, a Spanish market research startup, has raised €1.5 million, about $1.7 million, in a pre-seed round. Baobab Ventures, Lanai Ventures, Acurio Ventures and Masia VC invested.


The company was co-founded by co-CEO Dani Diestre, Aniol Carreras and Jacob Bamio.


WHAT AUTENTIC AI DOES


Traditional qualitative research is slow and expensive. Recruiting participants, scheduling interviews, running them and analyzing the results can take weeks or months, and a single study can cost a large brand six figures.


Autentic AI uses AI interviewers to talk with hundreds of consumers and industry experts at the same time. Human researchers then interpret the findings and add context. Participants are verified and paid for their time, and every insight in a final report links to video evidence from the interviews, so clients can see exactly where a conclusion came from. Results can be segmented by age, region or product usage.


The company says it now runs about 1,000 interviews a day and expects to pass 400,000 by the end of 2026. It serves four sectors: consumer packaged goods, retail, pharmaceuticals and cosmetics, and strategy consulting and private equity.


THE PITCH


Diestre's argument is about frequency. When a study costs around €100,000 and takes three months, companies cannot run one every time they have a question. Autentic AI wants research to become something brands do weekly rather than a few times a year.


HOW THE MONEY WILL BE USED


The funding will go toward automating more of the research process and building Autentic AI's own network of verified consumers and industry experts. That would reduce its reliance on third-party survey panels, which are widely criticized for fraud and low-quality responses.


WHY IT MATTERS


Market research is one of the industries AI is changing fastest. A wave of startups is using conversational AI to replace surveys and focus groups, promising depth at survey-like speed and cost. Autentic AI's focus on verified participants and video-backed findings addresses the category's main weakness: whether clients can trust that the people being interviewed are real and that the AI's summaries reflect what they actually said.


For a pre-seed company, a daily volume of 1,000 interviews and clients across consumer goods, pharma and private equity is notable traction, and gives Autentic AI a base to build toward a larger raise.

item.content:encoded:
Atlas Atomics, a stealth nuclear energy startup co-founded and backed by Vivek Ramaswamy, has raised about $400 million in a Series A round at a valuation of roughly $1.9 billion, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter.


General Catalyst is leading the round, with Andreessen Horowitz participating. Atlas Atomics, General Catalyst and a16z declined to comment, so the terms have not been confirmed by the company.


Who Is Behind Atlas Atomics


Ramaswamy, the entrepreneur and Ohio gubernatorial candidate, is a co-founder and backer. Day-to-day leadership sits with co-founder Kevin Gan, who spent more than 15 years investing in energy companies, most recently at hedge fund Millennium and before that at D.E. Shaw & Co.


The company's chief nuclear officer is Balendra Sutharshan, a former chief operating officer of Oak Ridge National Laboratory, the Department of Energy's largest science and energy lab and a central institution in American nuclear research. VentureTerminal lists the company in Columbus, Ohio.


The Technology


Atlas Atomics is developing an improved heavy water reactor. Unlike most reactors operating in the US, heavy water designs can run on natural uranium rather than enriched uranium. That matters because enrichment is expensive and global capacity is concentrated in a handful of suppliers, with Russia historically among the largest.


Avoiding enrichment could make Atlas's reactors cheaper to fuel and less exposed to supply bottlenecks. In a letter to Utah's Governor's Office of Energy Development, Gan said the technology aims to provide reliable power, expand production of medical and industrial isotopes and support nuclear fuel recycling.


Why It Matters


A $400 million Series A is one of the largest early-stage rounds in nuclear energy, and it arrives as demand for round-the-clock, carbon-free power climbs, driven largely by AI data centers. Tech companies have signed deals to restart old reactors and back new designs, and investors have followed with large checks into advanced nuclear startups.


Heavy water reactors are not new. Canada's CANDU fleet has run on the approach for decades. That track record could help with regulators, though any new design still faces a long licensing process with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. For Ohio, the company's ties to the state add to a growing presence in energy and advanced manufacturing investment.


Valuing a stealth company at nearly $2 billion before it has publicly shown a reactor is a large bet on its team. With a former Oak Ridge executive running the nuclear program and two of venture capital's biggest firms behind it, Atlas Atomics has the money and credibility to make its case.

item.title: How Much Did Myca Raise? Inside the $1.3M Pre-Seed Round
item.description: Myca, an Indian startup building AI software for agribusinesses, has raised $1.3 million in a pre-seed round. Kriscore Capital, Eximius Ventures and Indigram Labs Foundation backed the company, according to a report from The SaaS News . The funding will support the expansion of Myca's AI platform...
item.content:encoded:
Myca, an Indian startup building AI software for agribusinesses, has raised $1.3 million in a pre-seed round. Kriscore Capital, Eximius Ventures and Indigram Labs Foundation backed the company, according to a report from The SaaS News.


The funding will support the expansion of Myca's AI platform, which is aimed at companies that sell to, buy from and lend to farmers.


What Myca Does


Myca builds AI tools for the businesses that operate around the farm: input sellers, buyers, lenders and others whose work depends on staff travelling from village to village. Its software takes the information gathered in the field and turns it into structured business processes.


In practice, that means automating work such as sales, surveys and credit operations. These are tasks that agribusinesses have traditionally handled with large field teams, paper forms and phone calls. Myca's pitch is that a company can extend its reach across more villages without adding staff at the same rate, keeping operating costs steady as it grows.


The Founders Behind Myca


Myca was founded by Arnav Pandey, who serves as CEO, Seamus Tardif, the chief revenue officer, and Tejas Dinkar, the chief technology officer. The team combines experience in agriculture and in technology.


Why Field Data Is the Core Problem


Agriculture in emerging markets runs on fragmented information. A single agribusiness may deal with thousands of smallholder farmers spread over a wide area, each with different crops, land sizes and needs. Knowing who bought what, who needs a visit and who is a good credit risk depends on data that is often incomplete or locked in a field agent's notebook.


That gap is most costly in lending. Without reliable records, lenders struggle to assess farmers and to recover loans, which keeps credit expensive or unavailable. Myca's longer-term aim is for better structured field data to improve credit scoring and loan recovery, replacing manual systems with AI-driven coordination and risk assessment.


How Myca Will Use the $1.3M


The company plans to use the pre-seed capital to expand its AI platform for the agribusiness industry. Its ambitions extend beyond India: Myca has outlined plans to launch across Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa as well as its home market.


Those regions share the same basic structure, with large numbers of small farms served by businesses that rely on field staff. A product that works in rural India has a plausible path into each of them.


Why the Myca Funding Matters


Much of the first wave of agritech investment went to marketplaces and farmer-facing apps, many of which proved expensive to scale. Myca is taking a different angle by selling software to the agribusinesses themselves, which already have the farmer relationships and the budgets.


It is an early-stage bet, and a $1.3 million round is small. But it reflects a wider shift in how investors approach AI: away from general-purpose tools and toward products built for the workflows of a single industry, where the data is messy and the incumbents have been slow to modernize.


Source


The SaaS News — "Myca Raises $1.3M Pre-seed"

item.title: Can Light Beat Nvidia? Volantis Raises $88M for Photonic AI Chips
item.description: Volantis, a San Francisco semiconductor company building AI inference systems that move data with light, has raised an $88 million Series A co-led by Lachy Groom and Abstract Ventures. The company announced the round as it works toward delivering its first integrated inference engines in 2027. Jo...
item.content:encoded:
Volantis, a San Francisco semiconductor company building AI inference systems that move data with light, has raised an $88 million Series A co-led by Lachy Groom and Abstract Ventures. The company announced the round as it works toward delivering its first integrated inference engines in 2027.


John Doerr, VXI Capital, Triatomic and Susa Ventures also invested, along with angel investors Dwarkesh Patel, Naveen Rao and Sholto Douglas.


WHAT VOLANTIS IS BUILDING


Volantis is going after what chip designers call the memory wall. As AI models grow, the limiting factor in running them is often not how fast a processor can compute but how quickly data can travel between the processor and memory. Electrical connections can only carry so much, and that ceiling restricts both model size and response speed.


The company's answer is photonics, using light in place of electrical signals to connect chips to memory. Its first system, called A-1, combines custom micro-VCSELs, a type of very small laser, with photonic interconnects designed specifically for chip-to-memory links.


Volantis says the architecture will let models exceeding 20 trillion parameters run at up to 10,000 tokens per second per user while lowering the cost of inference. Those are company targets for a system that has not yet shipped, and they would represent a substantial leap over what current hardware delivers.


THE TEAM BEHIND VOLANTIS


Volantis is led by CEO and co-founder Tapa Ghosh. The team includes veterans of NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and Ayar Labs, with experience spanning CoWoS advanced packaging products, tunable VCSELs and silicon photonics systems.


"Today's hardware forces a tradeoff between running the largest models and running them fast. We started Volantis to eliminate that tradeoff," Ghosh said in the announcement.


HOW VOLANTIS WILL USE THE $88M


The funding will go toward developing and commercializing A-1, expanding the engineering team and preparing for customer deployments. The company is targeting 2027 for delivery of its first integrated inference engines.


An $88 million Series A is large by most standards but in line with what chip startups require. Designing, fabricating and packaging custom silicon and optics is capital intensive well before any revenue arrives.


WHY THE VOLANTIS FUNDING MATTERS


Most attention in AI hardware has centered on training, the process of building models. Inference, the work of running them for users, is where spending is shifting as AI products reach large audiences. Each query carries a cost, and that cost determines which products are viable.


Hardware that serves larger models faster and more cheaply would change that math. It is why investors continue to fund alternatives to conventional GPU systems, and why photonics, long confined to networking between servers, is now being pushed closer to the chip.


The investor list reflects that conviction. Doerr is one of Silicon Valley's best-known venture investors, Rao has founded AI chip companies of his own, and Patel and Douglas are closely followed voices in AI research circles.


Volantis still has to prove its design in production silicon. If A-1 performs as described, it would give AI developers a new way around one of the hardest constraints in the field.


SOURCE


PR Newswire — "Volantis Raises $88M Series A to Demolish the AI Memory Wall With Photonics"

item.title: How Much Did Promenaut Raise? Inside the $8.9M HSBC-Backed Round
item.description: Promenaut, a startup building software that manages people and AI agents as a single governed workforce, has launched with $8.9 million in total funding and HSBC as both an investor and a design partner. The company announced its platform and the HSBC relationship together, positioning itself for...
item.content:encoded:
Promenaut, a startup building software that manages people and AI agents as a single governed workforce, has launched with $8.9 million in total funding and HSBC as both an investor and a design partner. The company announced its platform and the HSBC relationship together, positioning itself for regulated industries where putting AI agents into production requires more than a capable model.


The bank is not just writing a check. HSBC is already running Promenaut in production, and its Chief AI Officer, David Rice, has joined the startup's board.


What Promenaut Does


Promenaut describes its product as an enterprise agentic workforce platform. In plain terms, it is an orchestration layer that assigns, tracks and supervises work across human employees and AI agents, treating both as parts of one workforce rather than as separate systems.


The platform is built around the controls that banks and other regulated firms need before they can let agents act: audit trails that record what was done and why, human oversight checkpoints, and governance rules that set what an agent can and cannot do. It is model-agnostic and runs across any cloud environment, so customers are not tied to a single AI provider.


How HSBC Is Using Promenaut


HSBC has deployed the platform for specialized workflows, including business case evaluation and the pre-coding steps in software delivery, the planning and specification work that happens before engineers begin writing code. Those are document-heavy, review-heavy processes where agents can take on preparation while people retain sign-off.


For an early-stage company, having a global bank as a live production customer, an investor and a board-level participant is a meaningful endorsement. It also gives Promenaut a demanding environment in which to prove its governance model.


Who Is Behind Promenaut


The company is led by CEO and co-founder Stephen Murphy, who has spent more than 25 years solving technology problems for large financial institutions. Promenaut is based in the United States and maintains a significant presence in London.


Murphy frames agent orchestration as something enterprises need to control directly rather than hand to a vendor. "The firms that treat that as something they own will end up in a very different position to those that don't," he said in the announcement.


Why the Promenaut Funding Matters


Most large companies have run AI pilots. Far fewer have agents doing real work inside core operations, and the gap is rarely about model quality. It is about accountability: who approved an action, what data the agent touched, and how the firm demonstrates that to a regulator.


Promenaut is betting that this governance layer becomes its own software category. If agents are going to be treated as workers, enterprises will need a system of record for what those workers do, sitting alongside the tools already used to manage human teams.


The $8.9 million gives the company runway to extend the platform beyond its first design partner. HSBC's involvement gives it something harder to buy: a reference customer in one of the most heavily regulated industries in the world.

Promenaut — "Promenaut Launches Enterprise Agentic Workforce Platform; Announces HSBC Investment and Collaboration"

item.title: Project Suppliers Raises $1M Pre-Seed to Build AI Cash Flow Tools for Saudi Construction
item.description: Project Suppliers, a Saudi Arabian technology platform that connects buyers and suppliers in the construction industry, has closed a SAR 3.75 million pre-seed round, equal to $1 million. The money came from a group of angel investors whose names were not disclosed. The company plans to use the fu...
item.content:encoded:
Project Suppliers, a Saudi Arabian technology platform that connects buyers and suppliers in the construction industry, has closed a SAR 3.75 million pre-seed round, equal to $1 million. The money came from a group of angel investors whose names were not disclosed.


The company plans to use the funding to develop AI-powered cash flow management tools for contractors and suppliers, a move that would take it from marketplace into financial services.


What Project Suppliers Does


Project Suppliers focuses on construction and on MEP, the mechanical, electrical and plumbing work that makes up a large share of any building project. Contractors use the platform to send quotation requests to suppliers and to manage parts of their supply chain digitally, replacing a process that still runs largely on phone calls, messaging apps and spreadsheets.


The company says its database covers more than 12,000 suppliers and contractors, and that nearly 600,000 quotation requests have been submitted through the platform. The round was also covered by The SaaS News.


From Marketplace to Cash Flow


That volume of requests is the foundation for the next product. Every quotation records who is buying what, from whom, at what price and on what schedule. Project Suppliers intends to use that operational data to build intelligent financing and predictive analytics tools aimed at one of the industry's most persistent problems: liquidity.


Construction runs on long payment cycles. Contractors often pay for materials well before they are paid for the finished work, and suppliers extend credit without a clear view of when the money will arrive. Late payment moves down the chain and can stall projects. Tools that forecast cash needs and match financing to real purchasing activity could ease that pressure for the small and mid-sized firms that feel it most.


Co-founder and CEO Hossam Gaber described the Saudi market as an exceptional opportunity for technological and financial change in the sector.


Why It Matters


Saudi Arabia is in the middle of one of the largest building programs in the world, driven by Vision 2030 and its slate of giga-projects. That activity has made construction technology a growing area for startups in the Kingdom, especially those tackling procurement and financing.


The model Project Suppliers is pursuing has worked in other markets: start with a marketplace that captures transactions, then use the resulting data to offer credit and financial tools that banks have trouble underwriting on their own. A $1 million pre-seed is a modest sum, and the company still has to show that its quotation data can support reliable lending decisions. With a base of suppliers and contractors already on the platform, it starts that effort with a clear view of how money moves through the sector.


Source


Entarabi — "Project Suppliers Closes SAR 3.75 Million Pre-Seed Investment Round to Develop AI-Powered Cash Flow Management Solutions"

item.title: Can AI Replace Penetration Testers? Fleuret AI Raises $4.7M
item.description: Fleuret AI, a Paris-based cybersecurity startup, has raised €4 million, about $4.7 million, in a pre-seed round led by RAISE Ventures. Auriga Cyber Ventures, Wind and Better Angle also invested, along with business angels from the cybersecurity sector. The company is building an agentic AI platfo...
item.content:encoded:
Fleuret AI, a Paris-based cybersecurity startup, has raised €4 million, about $4.7 million, in a pre-seed round led by RAISE Ventures. Auriga Cyber Ventures, Wind and Better Angle also invested, along with business angels from the cybersecurity sector.


The company is building an agentic AI platform that automates penetration testing, the practice of attacking a company's own systems to find weaknesses before criminals do.


WHAT FLEURET AI DOES


Traditional penetration tests are usually performed by outside specialists on a set schedule, often once or twice a year. The result is a snapshot. Software changes weekly, and a vulnerability introduced the day after an audit can sit undiscovered for months.


Fleuret AI wants to turn that periodic exercise into a continuous process. Its platform covers five steps: mapping the systems a company exposes to the internet, identifying vulnerabilities, demonstrating that those vulnerabilities can actually be exploited, supporting the fix, and then re-testing to confirm the fix worked. Two AI agents, named Emile and Champollion, do the exploring, working through applications, APIs and infrastructure to find and test weak points.


The platform also prioritizes findings and connects with the tools security teams already use, so that results reach the people responsible for fixing them.


THE FOUNDERS AND THE SOVEREIGNTY ANGLE


Fleuret AI was founded by CEO Yanis Grigy and CTO Augustin Ponsin. Grigy has said the goal is not simply to automate penetration testing in its current form, but to build an offensive security layer that keeps companies protected throughout the year.


The startup runs on European infrastructure, a deliberate choice for customers with data sovereignty requirements. Tech Funding News reported that the platform is hosted with French cloud provider Scaleway. For European banks, public agencies and critical infrastructure operators, where sensitive security data is stored can decide whether a vendor is considered at all.


HOW THE MONEY WILL BE USED


The funding will be used to hire across AI, software development and offensive cybersecurity, and to speed up development of the platform for large enterprise environments.


WHY IT MATTERS


Automated offensive security has become one of the busiest corners of cybersecurity investing. AI agents can now chain together the steps of an attack in ways that once required a skilled human tester, and that capability is available to attackers as well as defenders. Companies face pressure to test their defenses far more often than a yearly audit allows, and skilled penetration testers remain scarce and expensive.


A $4.7 million pre-seed is a sizable first round by European standards, and it reflects how much investor interest the category is drawing. Fleuret AI's bet is that a European-hosted product, built for continuous testing from the start, can win customers who are wary of sending details of their vulnerabilities to providers outside the region.


SOURCE


Tech.eu — "Fleuret AI raises €4M to advance AI-powered offensive cybersecurity in Europe"

item.title: What Is Pandektes? The AI Legal Research Startup Raising $15.8M
item.description: Pandektes, a Copenhagen-based legal research startup, has raised €13.5 million, about $15.8 million, in a Series A round led by Munich-based Alstin Capital. PROfounders and Scale Capital also joined the round alongside existing investors. The raise was first reported by The Next Web. The funding ...
item.content:encoded:
Pandektes, a Copenhagen-based legal research startup, has raised €13.5 million, about $15.8 million, in a Series A round led by Munich-based Alstin Capital. PROfounders and Scale Capital also joined the round alongside existing investors. The raise was first reported by The Next Web.


The funding follows a €2.9 million seed round announced in February 2025 and comes after a year in which the company says its revenue grew sixfold.


WHAT PANDEKTES DOES


Pandektes builds an AI-powered research platform for lawyers. It gathers legislation, court decisions and administrative rulings into one place, structures that material and links related documents together, so that a lawyer looking for relevant case law can search across sources that are normally scattered among government sites and legacy databases. The platform can also combine those public sources with a client's own data.


The company was founded by CEO Casper Laursen and Søren Brokær. Its pitch is that the quality of any AI legal product depends on the data underneath it, and that the foundational work of collecting and organizing legal information is where a lasting advantage is built.


GROWTH SO FAR


Pandektes is active in Denmark, Germany and Switzerland and says it is used by more than 500 law firms, companies and public institutions. That is up from roughly 100 organizations around the time of its seed round. According to the company, about two of every three organizations that trial the product become paying customers.


Those numbers helped draw Alstin Capital. Managing partner Andreas Schenk told The Next Web that legal research is an unusual market, one where many users have long wanted to replace their core system and had no practical alternative.


HOW THE MONEY WILL BE USED


The company plans to use the Series A to expand beyond its three current markets into more of Europe and into North America, and to grow its team. As EU-Startups reported, Pandektes also intends to open its data through an API, allowing third-party developers to build their own legal tools on top of its infrastructure.


That last piece signals a broader ambition. Rather than competing only as a search product for law firms, Pandektes wants to become the data layer that other legal AI products rely on.


WHY IT MATTERS


Legal research has been dominated for decades by a small number of incumbent database providers. Generative AI has opened the category to challengers, and investors have poured money into legal tech as a result. Most of that attention has gone to AI assistants that draft and review documents. Pandektes is working on the layer below: clean, connected, current legal data, country by country.


That work is slow and specific to each jurisdiction, which makes it harder to copy. If the company can repeat its Nordic and German-speaking results in larger markets, a $15.8 million Series A gives it a base from which to challenge much bigger rivals.


SOURCE


The Next Web — "Exclusive: Danish legal research startup Pandektes raises €13.5M Series A"

item.title: OneByZero Raises $20M Series A Led by Jungle Ventures to Scale Enterprise AI
item.description: OneByZero, a Singapore-based company that deploys artificial intelligence inside large and regulated enterprises, has raised $20 million in a Series A round led by Jungle Ventures. The round is the company's first outside funding, coming after three years of building its business on revenue from ...
item.content:encoded:
OneByZero, a Singapore-based company that deploys artificial intelligence inside large and regulated enterprises, has raised $20 million in a Series A round led by Jungle Ventures. The round is the company's first outside funding, coming after three years of building its business on revenue from enterprise customers.


The raise lands as big companies across Asia Pacific struggle with a familiar problem: AI pilots are easy to start and hard to turn into systems that run day to day. OneByZero is betting that the fix is less about the model and more about the engineering work required to wire it into a business.


What OneByZero Does


OneByZero uses a forward-deployed model. Its engineers work on site with a customer's teams to identify the use cases worth pursuing, build AI into existing workflows and systems, and keep improving those deployments once they are live. Its customers so far sit mainly in financial services, telecommunications and retail, sectors where compliance and legacy infrastructure tend to slow new technology down.


Behind those teams is NEO, the company's AI deployment platform. NEO provides governance controls and audit trails, and it manages what OneByZero calls AI Coworkers: AI agents assigned defined roles and limits so that a regulated business can track what each one is allowed to do.


Traction Before the Raise


The company says its revenue has more than doubled every year for the past three years. It also reports that some deployments have automated more than 90% of certain customer-facing interactions, and that its work has cut delivery time on complex data modernization projects by half. Those figures are the company's own.


OneByZero currently operates in nine markets: Australia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, the United States and Vietnam. It was founded by CEO Niket Vaidya and CTO Vibhore Kumar.


How the Money Will Be Used


The new capital will go toward expanding the forward-deployed engineering teams in the markets where the company already works, and toward opening operations in Japan. According to Tech Edition, OneByZero also plans to move into additional industries, including conglomerates, healthcare and the public sector, while continuing to develop NEO and its AI Coworkers.


Vaidya has framed the opportunity around execution. Access to capable AI is now widely available, in his view, and the value shows up only once it is running inside the systems a business depends on.


Why It Matters


Enterprise AI spending has shifted from experimentation toward production, and that shift favors firms that can do the integration work. The forward-deployed approach, pairing software with engineers who sit alongside the customer, has become one of the more closely watched models in the sector because it addresses the gap between a working demo and a governed system in production.


For Jungle Ventures, one of Southeast Asia's most active venture firms, the deal is a bet that the region's banks, telcos and retailers will pay for that help. For OneByZero, a $20 million Series A after three years of customer-funded growth gives it the resources to hire ahead of demand and test its model in Japan, one of the largest enterprise technology markets in Asia.


Source


e27 — "OneByZero raises US$20M Series A to help enterprises move AI from pilots to production"

item.title: Clockout Raises $3.5M to Build a Professional Networking App for Gen Z
item.description: Clockout, a networking app that helps people meet nearby professionals in person, has raised $3.5 million to date in funding led by 114 Ventures. The company and its 32-year-old founder and CEO, Krishna Dosapati, were profiled by Fortune , which framed the startup as a response to the isolation m...
item.content:encoded:
Clockout, a networking app that helps people meet nearby professionals in person, has raised $3.5 million to date in funding led by 114 Ventures. The company and its 32-year-old founder and CEO, Krishna Dosapati, were profiled by Fortune, which framed the startup as a response to the isolation many younger workers describe as they enter the workforce.


Evite Ventures, Allied Ventures, Sher Ventures, Gaingels and BMPB VC are among the other investors backing the company.


What Clockout Does


Clockout sits somewhere between LinkedIn and Meetup. Users can discover professionals near them, join communities organized around an industry or a shared interest, and find local events to attend. The emphasis is on meeting in real life rather than collecting connections on a profile page.


That positioning targets a gap in the market. LinkedIn is built for job searches, recruiting and content, while event platforms are organized around the gathering instead of the ongoing relationship. Clockout is trying to own the space where a professional network and a social circle overlap.


The Founder Behind Clockout


Dosapati graduated from New York University and stayed in New York to work, where she ran into the problem firsthand. Building a network in a new city, without a campus or an established circle to lean on, proved harder than expected.


"If I faced this, how are younger people going to build their network, make friends and find a professional community?" she told Fortune.


The question has only become more pressing as remote and hybrid work reduce the casual office contact that once helped early-career employees find mentors and friends.


Clockout Traction and Revenue


Clockout launched in October 2024 and has since passed 600,000 downloads. The company reached $1.1 million in annual recurring revenue within 10 months of turning on monetization, an unusually quick path to revenue for a consumer social product. Users sent 400,000 invitations through the app in 2025.


The business runs on a freemium model. The core app is free, and a $99 annual subscription unlocks premium features. Subscription revenue means Clockout does not have to rely solely on advertising, the model that has shaped most social platforms.


Why the Clockout Funding Matters


Consumer social has been a difficult category for venture investors, with few new networks breaking through against entrenched incumbents. Clockout's early numbers suggest that a narrower promise, meet useful people near you, can succeed where broader social apps have stalled.


The startup is also arriving as concern about loneliness among Gen Z draws attention from employers and investors alike. A product that turns online discovery into in-person connection speaks directly to that concern, and paying subscribers indicate users see real value in it.


With $3.5 million raised and recurring revenue already above $1 million, Clockout has room to grow its communities and events city by city without the cash burn that has sunk other social startups.


Source


Fortune — "Meet the 32-year-old founder who raised $3.5 million to help Gen Z feel not so alone in the world"

item.title: Is SiMa.ai Worth $1.45B? Inside the $150M Series C
item.description: SiMa.ai, the San Jose chipmaker building silicon for robots and cameras rather than data centers, has raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation. Fidelity Management & Research Company and Amplify led the round. Alter Venture Partners, Dell Technologies Capital and StepStone Grou...
item.content:encoded:
SiMa.ai, the San Jose chipmaker building silicon for robots and cameras rather than data centers, has raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation. Fidelity Management & Research Company and Amplify led the round.


Alter Venture Partners, Dell Technologies Capital and StepStone Group also participated. Total capital raised now exceeds $500 million.


AI Without the Cloud


SiMa.ai makes energy-efficient chips and the software around them so devices can run AI models on-device, with no round trip to a data center.


That matters for anything that has to react in real time. A drone avoiding an obstacle or a robot arm adjusting its grip cannot wait on a network request, and many industrial deployments have no reliable connectivity at all.


The company was founded by CEO Krishna Rangasayee, previously chief operating officer at chipmaker Groq.


The Valuation Jump


The $1.45 billion valuation is up from $960 million at the company's Series B in July 2025.


TechCrunch reported the raise, noting the company is betting that low-latency performance and lower cost relative to Nvidia GPUs will win it share of the physical AI market, including humanoid robots.


The Physical AI Race


"Physical AI" has become the industry's shorthand for models that control machines in the world rather than generate text on a screen, and it has drawn a wave of capital across chips, robots and simulation.


The chip layer is the most capital-intensive part of it. Designing silicon, taping out and qualifying customers takes years, which is why a company at this stage has already raised more than half a billion dollars.


Why It Matters


Nvidia dominates AI training and much of inference in the data center, but edge devices have different constraints: tight power budgets, fixed costs per unit and physical space limits.


That gap is what independent chipmakers are targeting. SiMa.ai's pitch is efficiency and price, and with Dell Technologies Capital on the cap table it has at least one investor who knows what device makers will pay for.


Source


TechCrunch — "Physical AI chip developer SiMa AI hits $1.45B valuation"

item.title: How Much Did Quartermaster Raise? Inside the $140M Series B
item.description: Quartermaster, an Arlington, Virginia company that turns commercial ships into ocean sensors, has raised a $140 million Series B led by Insight Partners. Overmatch Ventures joined as a new investor and First Round Capital returned, alongside a $40 million debt facility from Stifel. Sensors on the...
item.content:encoded:
Quartermaster, an Arlington, Virginia company that turns commercial ships into ocean sensors, has raised a $140 million Series B led by Insight Partners. Overmatch Ventures joined as a new investor and First Round Capital returned, alongside a $40 million debt facility from Stifel.


Sensors on the Mast


The company's product, SmartMast, is a weather-hardened package of cameras and radios that mounts on a ship's mast and streams data back. Each unit generates tens of gigabytes a day.


Put enough of them on enough hulls and the result is a picture of activity at sea that satellites, with their revisit gaps, cannot provide continuously.


Quartermaster says SmartMast is installed on more than 650 vessels across 25 countries, with over 800 units shipped.


Why Now


Demand has been driven by events rather than sales cycles. Attacks on commercial shipping and disruptions to sea lanes have made real-time maritime awareness an operational requirement for fleet operators and governments alike.


"A big part of the story for us this year was, events in the world drive that clarity and urgency, and when you see that, you gotta seize the opportunity," said CEO Neil Sobin.


TechCrunch first reported the round, the company's second large raise of the year.

Where the Money Goes


Quartermaster is doubling manufacturing capacity to meet demand and moving from ship-by-ship installs to fleet-wide deployments.


"Quartermaster is building a distributed network for the ocean, where reliable, real-time data has been difficult to come by," said Nick Sinai of Insight Partners.


Why It Matters


The economics resemble other sensor-network businesses: the hardware is the entry point, but the value compounds as coverage grows, because each additional ship improves the overall picture.


That also makes this a race for installed base. The $40 million debt facility alongside the equity says the constraint right now is building units fast enough, not finding buyers.


Source


TechCrunch — "Maritime intelligence startup Quartermaster raises another $140M"

item.title: How Much Did Modulate Raise? Inside the $25M Audio AI Round
item.description: Modulate, a Boston company building AI that listens to conversations rather than just transcribing them, has raised $25 million led by Future Ventures, with Hyperplane and Lakestar participating. The company was founded by Mike Pappas and Carter Huffman, who met as physics undergraduates at MIT. ...
item.content:encoded:
Modulate, a Boston company building AI that listens to conversations rather than just transcribing them, has raised $25 million led by Future Ventures, with Hyperplane and Lakestar participating.


The company was founded by Mike Pappas and Carter Huffman, who met as physics undergraduates at MIT. It had previously raised $41 million at a $170 million valuation.


Past the Transcript


Modulate first became known for ToxMod, a voice moderation tool used to catch harassment in online games. The company has since broadened into a voice intelligence platform: transcription plus emotional analysis, deepfake and AI-music detection, and policy enforcement for voice agents.


"Our insight into the voice AI space is that a lot of folks are doing transcription, but there's not really any capability out there that gets the full nuance and full understanding of a conversation," Huffman said.


The company says it has more than 100 models deployed.


Where It Sells


The commercial focus is call centers and enterprises running AI customer service, with particular attention to regulated industries where what was said, and how, carries compliance weight.


Huffman points to a limitation of text-only analysis: "Many times people will be polite even to AI agents or bots," he said, "but they'll be very dissatisfied." A transcript scores that call as fine. The audio does not.


Where the Money Goes


Modulate plans to strengthen its model-building capability and expand on-premises and on-device deployment for customers who cannot send audio to a vendor's cloud. The company has 40 to 45 employees and plans to hire about 10 more.


TechCrunch reported the raise, covering the voice models and analysis suite.


Why It Matters


As companies hand more customer conversations to AI agents, someone has to evaluate how those conversations are actually going. Deepfaked voices also make verification a live problem for any business that authenticates people by phone.


Both needs point at audio-native analysis rather than text pipelines, and Modulate has the advantage of years of voice data from a moderation product that had to work in the messiest conditions available: live game chat.

item.title: How to Top Up Rapid Rewards for a Last-Minute Flight
item.description: Disclosure: YourInfoDaily may earn a commission if you buy through links in this article. If you are a few thousand Rapid Rewards points short of a flight, buy the missing points while a discount is runn...
item.content:encoded:
Disclosure: YourInfoDaily may earn a commission if you buy through links in this article. Offers change and are often targeted, so confirm the terms in your own account before buying.


If you are a few thousand Rapid Rewards points short of a flight, buy the missing points while a discount is running, then book right away. If the flight leaves within hours and you cannot wait for points to arrive, use Southwest's Cash + Points option or pay the fare. Those are the two paths, and the rest of this guide helps you choose.

Start with the numbers

Southwest ties award prices to cash fares, and last-minute fares are usually the highest. Frequent Miler notes that the points needed rise with demand. Check the price now, since it may have moved since you last looked.

Write down:

  • The points price for the flight.
  • Your current balance.
  • The cash fare.


The first minus the second is your gap. The third is your fallback.

Option 1: Buy the missing points

Southwest sells Rapid Rewards points for 3 cents each at the standard price and often discounts them. One Mile at a Time reported a sale from September 2 to October 2, 2026, with discounts of 35%, 45%, or 50% depending on the member, and Award Travel Finder listed a 50% discount running through October 29, 2026. Your account shows which offer, if any, applies to you.


The September sale discount required a purchase of at least 3,000 points. What that costs:

  • At 50% off: about $45.
  • At 45% off: about $50.
  • At 35% off: about $59.
  • At full price: $90.

Larger gaps, at 50% off:

  • 5,000 points: about $75.
  • 10,000 points: about $150.

According to One Mile at a Time, you can buy up to 60,000 points per day, with no annual limit.


Timing: allow time for the points to reach your account. Posting times vary, so don't buy with minutes to spare. If your departure is within a few hours, go to Option 2.


Check your Rapid Rewards points offer.


Option 2: Cash + Points

Southwest lets you pay for a ticket with a mix of cash and points. Nothing has to post first, so it works for last-minute trips.


The drawback is value. Frequent Miler says this option yields poor value per point. Use it when time is the constraint, not as a habit.


Option 3: Have someone else book it

Southwest lets members book award flights for other people. If a partner, parent, or bandmate has enough points, they can book your seat from their account, and you can settle up between yourselves.


This is usually better than asking them to transfer points to you, because Southwest charges a fee for transfers between members.


Option 4: Pay cash and keep your points

Sometimes the best top-up is none. Divide the cash fare by the points price. Frequent Miler benchmarks a Rapid Rewards point at 1.3 cents, and One Mile at a Time estimates 1.1 to 1.5 cents. If your flight gives you less than that per point, pay the fare, earn points, and save your balance for better use.


Which should you pick?

  • Short by 3,000 points or less, with a day or more to spare: buy during a discount.
  • If you have hours left: Cash + Points, or pay the fare.
  • Someone you trust has points: ask them to book.
  • Short by 10,000 or more: run the cash comparison first. A big purchase at 1.5 cents or more per point rarely beats paying the fare.


A worked example

These are illustrative numbers. A Friday flight costs $289 or 21,500 points. You have 19,000 points.

  • Buy 3,000 points at 50% off: about $45 out of pocket. You fly for $45 plus taxes and keep 500 points.
  • Pay cash: $289, and your 19,000 points stay unused.


Here the top-up is the obvious choice. It saves about $244 compared with paying the fare.


Change one number. You have only 6,000 points and need 15,500 more. At 50% off, that costs about $233, close to the $289 fare, and you would drain your balance. Paying cash and earning points on the trip is the better move.


Why points are useful for uncertain plans

Frequent Miler notes that Southwest award flights can be canceled with no fee up to 10 minutes before departure, and the points come back to your account immediately. One Mile at a Time adds that a canceled cash ticket becomes a travel credit for a future flight.


For a last-minute trip that might still fall through, a points booking is easier to undo. That is a real reason to top up even when the math is only slightly in your favor.


Small print

  • Rapid Rewards points don't expire, so leftovers from a top-up will stay.
  • Purchased points do not count toward the Companion Pass.
  • Points.com processes the purchase, so your card will not treat it as airfare.
  • Free checked bags now depend on your fare, status, or Southwest card. Include bag fees when comparing a Southwest fare with another airline's.


Top up your Rapid Rewards balance and book.


FAQ

What is the minimum number of Southwest points I can buy?

The recent discount applied to purchases of at least 3,000 points. Check your account for the current minimum.


Can I book a Southwest flight with points for a friend?

Yes. You can book award flights for others from your account.


Can I cancel a Southwest points booking?

Yes, with no fee up to 10 minutes before departure, and you get your points back.


Is Cash + Points a good deal?

Generally not on value, though it is useful when you are out of time.

item.content:encoded:
Tiny Health, an Austin company that sells at-home microbiome testing, has raised a $33 million Series B led by B Capital, bringing total funding to $46 million.


Spero Ventures, The Venture City, Overwater Ventures, Black Opal Ventures, Denver Ventures, Pave Health Ventures, Alumni Ventures, Gaingels and Pari Passu Ventures also participated.


From Infants to Adults


Tiny Health launched around infant gut testing, built by founder and CEO Cheryl Sew Hoy after looking for answers about her own family.


"What started as a solution for my own family has become the infrastructure for an entire industry," Sew Hoy said.


The company now offers gut and vaginal microbiome testing across the lifespan, using shotgun metagenomic sequencing paired with its own AI analysis. Adult testing volume has passed pediatric.


The Numbers


Tiny Health reports roughly 200,000 customers and more than 6,000 healthcare practitioners using its results. Its B2B platform, Powered by Tiny, grew fourfold year over year.


"Tiny Health has built the platform best positioned to bring that science... to patients, providers, and partners at scale," said Nick Whitehead of B Capital.


Where the Money Goes


The funding goes toward clinical research, practitioner education, scaling the B2B platform, accelerating its TinyAI work and a $5 million Microbiome Research Program.


That research spending is the notable line. Microbiome testing has faced persistent criticism that consumer results outrun the underlying evidence, and funding studies is the direct answer to it.


MedCity News covered the raise as funding to expand microbiome testing.


Why It Matters


Selling tests directly to consumers is a different business from becoming part of clinical care, and Tiny Health is trying to move from the first to the second. Practitioner adoption and the B2B platform are the bridge.


Whether microbiome data changes what a clinician actually does, rather than adding an interesting report, is the question the research program has to answer.

item.title: What If Robots Could Actually Feel? TacnIQ’s $1.5M Raise Aims to Find Out
item.description: TacnIQ.ai has raised $1.5 million from In Group Holdings as part of a $3 million pre-seed round, money the company will use to build foundation models for touch — the sense that most of the current AI boom has skipped. The gap the company is aiming at Vision and language models have gotten very g...
item.content:encoded:
TacnIQ.ai has raised $1.5 million from In Group Holdings as part of a $3 million pre-seed round, money the company will use to build foundation models for touch — the sense that most of the current AI boom has skipped.


The gap the company is aiming at

Vision and language models have gotten very good. Machines that must make physical contact with the world haven't benefited nearly as much. A robot arm can identify a box on a shelf and still fail to pick it up, because knowing what something looks like says little about how much it weighs, how it deforms under pressure, or when a grip is about to slip.


TacnIQ.ai's argument is that this is a data problem before it is a model problem. Tactile datasets are scarce, fragmented, and usually collected for one narrow application at a time, which means every new use case starts close to zero.


The dataset

The company says it has accumulated more than 5,000 hours of tactile interaction data from experiments and field deployments — what it describes as one of the larger tactile datasets currently available. The collection method is the clever part: sensor-based wearable nodes capture physical interactions as they happen in real work environments, not in a lab rig.

The strategic bet is on breadth. Rather than training a model per application, TacnIQ.ai is training across industries on multimodal data, on the theory that the underlying physics of contact generalizes even when the tasks do not.


Already shipping

Unusually for a pre-seed company in physical AI, the technology is already deployed with paying customers across logistics, construction, e-commerce, hospitality and healthcare. The current commercial hook is not autonomous robots — it is workplace safety and ergonomics, using the same contact data to flag movements and loads that injure workers.


That is a sensible wedge. Safety and workers' compensation costs are line items every operations director already budgets for, making it a far easier sale than a speculative automation roadmap.


Team and partners

Co-founder and CEO Aashish Mehta is running the company across Singapore and California. "Our mission is to build AI models that deliver real-world impact today and transform how engineers design and develop hardware," Mehta said.


The company is also working with Synaptics, the chip designer whose touch and sensing silicon shows up across consumer and industrial devices — a useful relationship for anyone trying to get tactile sensing into hardware at volume rather than as a bolt-on.


What the money buys

Funds will expand the engineering team, advance the tactile foundation models, and scale deployments into additional industrial applications.


The read

Physical AI has become a crowded pitch category, and most of it is still demo-stage. TacnIQ.ai's position is more defensible than most: a proprietary dataset that is genuinely hard to replicate, revenue from a use case that does not require the robotics market to mature first, and a chip partner. At $3 million, it is also cheap enough to find out. The risk is the one every foundation-model startup faces — whether a general tactile model actually outperforms purpose-built sensing in the specific jobs customers are paying for.

item.content:encoded:
Reco, a security company that tracks what AI agents are doing inside a company's software, has raised $55 million in a Series C extension with participation from AT&T Ventures, Forestay and Quadrille Capital. Total funding now stands at $140 million.


The company is led by co-founder and CEO Ofer Klein.


Finding the Agents Nobody Approved


Reco builds a context graph mapping which agents can reach which applications, people, accounts and permissions, across more than 280 SaaS integrations.


The problem it addresses is discovery. Employees connect agents to company systems without telling security, and those agents inherit real permissions. At one Fortune 100 customer, Reco says it found 21,000 agents nobody knew about. At a financial services firm, it identified a rogue agent reaching into Salesforce.


"The market demand right now for agent security is not only about the agent itself; it's about the entire ecosystem end-to-end," Klein said.


Growth


Reco says it has more than 100 customers, roughly 40% of them in financial services and including Fortune 100 companies. Annual recurring revenue is in the double-digit millions and the company expects it to triple this year.


Its valuation has more than doubled since a Series B in February. The funding goes toward hiring, sales, partnerships and customer support.


A Crowded Field


Agent security has become one of the most contested corners of cybersecurity, with established SaaS security vendors and a wave of startups all claiming the category. TechCrunch framed the raise against exactly that crowding.


Reco's argument is its starting point: it built SaaS discovery and posture management before agents were the story, and that integration footprint is what lets it see agent activity across applications rather than in one vendor's silo.


Why It Matters


Security teams spent a decade learning to inventory SaaS applications employees signed up for without approval. Agents are the same problem with higher stakes, because an agent does not just hold data, it takes actions.


An unknown agent with Salesforce write access is an operational risk, not a compliance footnote, and 21,000 of them at a single company explains why buyers are moving fast enough to triple a vendor's revenue in a year.
