item.title: Is Instinct Worth $10B? Inside the $1B Series C
item.description: Instinct, a San Francisco company building a personal AI agent, has raised $1 billion in a Series C from Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Coatue at a $10 billion valuation. The company was founded by Noah Shinn. An Agent With Its Own Phone Instinct is pitched as a personal agent rather than a chatb...
item.content:encoded:
Instinct, a San Francisco company building a personal AI agent, has raised $1 billion in a Series C from Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Coatue at a $10 billion valuation.


The company was founded by Noah Shinn.


An Agent With Its Own Phone


Instinct is pitched as a personal agent rather than a chatbot. It handles everyday errands, planning a trip, ordering groceries, canceling a subscription, using its own phone and computer access to carry tasks through to completion.


The distinction matters. Most consumer AI products answer questions and hand the work back. An agent that holds its own accounts and devices can finish the job, which also means it needs far more trust from the person it works for.


"We're building Instinct to be the best personal agent that can handle the deeply personal nuances of everyday life," Shinn said.


A Billion Dollars in Early Access


The product is still in early access, with no user numbers disclosed. A $1 billion round at a $10 billion valuation ahead of general availability is a bet on demand rather than a reflection of it.


"This funding helps us bring Instinct to more people and continue building the future of personal AI," Shinn said.


TechCrunch reported the round, describing the product as a viral AI agent.


Why Investors Moved


Sequoia, Benchmark and Coatue on one cap table is an unusual combination, and the size of the round suggests competition to get in rather than a company that needed the money.


The consumer AI assistant category has been the most-attempted and least-won part of the market. Every large platform has shipped one, and none has become the thing people reach for by default.


Why It Matters


If an agent can reliably complete transactions on a person's behalf, it sits between consumers and every business that sells to them, which is a commercially significant position and the reason valuations in this category run ahead of revenue.


The risks are equally concrete. An agent with payment and account access makes mistakes that cost real money, and consumer tolerance for that is low. Expanding from early access to general availability is where that gets tested.

item.title: How Much Did PicoJool Raise? Inside the $27.5M AI Optics Round
item.description: PicoJool, a Palo Alto company making the lasers that carry data between chips in AI data centers, has raised a $27.5 million Series A led by Socratic Partners, with Hudson River Trading participating. The round brings total funding to $39.5 million, including a $12 million seed. The company is le...
item.content:encoded:
PicoJool, a Palo Alto company making the lasers that carry data between chips in AI data centers, has raised a $27.5 million Series A led by Socratic Partners, with Hudson River Trading participating.


The round brings total funding to $39.5 million, including a $12 million seed. The company is led by CEO Al Yuen.


Lasers, Not Copper


PicoJool builds vertical cavity surface emitting lasers, or VCSELs, and smaller microVCSELs, the light sources behind optical links inside data centers.


Its products run from 50G to 200G per lane, with a roadmap the company says scales to 1.6T and beyond. Its 200G parts exceed 37GHz of bandwidth.


"Reaching 200G per lane proved that the performance is there. Our focus now is execution," Yuen said.


Where the Money Goes


PicoJool plans to expand teams and facilities in the United States and Taiwan, grow research, operations, sales and marketing, and build manufacturing capacity for product qualification and customer support.


Manufacturing is done with partner WIN Semiconductor, which the company notes has shipped more than a billion chips over the past decade.


HPCwire reported the raise as funding to scale optical connectivity for AI infrastructure.


Why Optics


As AI clusters grow, moving data between accelerators becomes as much of a constraint as the accelerators themselves. Electrical links over copper run into limits on reach, bandwidth and power, which has pushed the industry toward optical connections at ever shorter distances.


"Moving data efficiently dictates how quickly and economically AI scales," said Greg Waters, general partner at Socratic Partners.


Why It Matters


Optical interconnect has become one of the more crowded corners of AI infrastructure, with startups and established component makers all chasing the same hyperscaler qualification cycles.


PicoJool's position is at the light source rather than the full interconnect system, a component business where qualification and yield decide the winners. Hudson River Trading's participation is notable: the trading firm runs some of the most latency-sensitive infrastructure in finance.

item.content:encoded:
Outmarket AI has raised a $34.5 million Series B led by SignalFire at a $335 million valuation, just months after its previous round. Fika Ventures, Permanent Capital Ventures, TTV Capital and Dash Fund also participated.


The company, founded by CEO Vishal Sankhla, builds AI that handles paperwork and administrative work for commercial insurance agencies and brokers. Read his statement on below:

The Agent Still Runs Insurance


Software has reshaped how insurance is priced and underwritten, but distribution has barely moved. "Ninety-five percent of insurance in the U.S. and worldwide is still sold through [human] agents," Sankhla said, "and when you look at sort of like how the process is today, it's very manual."


That manual work is the target: submissions, certificates, endorsements and the constant document handling between an agency, its clients and carriers.


Growth in a Slow Industry


Outmarket says more than 300 insurance agencies now use the product, including about a quarter of the top 100. The product launched roughly 14 months before this round.


"For insurance, which is typically not a fast-moving industry, it's quite fast growth," Sankhla said.


TechCrunch reported the raise, noting it came only months after the prior round.


Why Agencies Buy


Commercial insurance agencies are people businesses with thin operating leverage: growth usually means hiring more account managers to process more paper. Software that absorbs document work changes that equation directly, which makes the return easy for an agency principal to calculate.


It also explains the pace. Agencies talk to each other, and in a referral-driven industry adoption can move faster than the sector's reputation suggests.


Why It Matters


Insurtech's first wave aimed at replacing incumbents with direct-to-consumer carriers, and most of those companies struggled with the economics of underwriting.


The current wave sells to the incumbents instead. Outmarket raising twice inside a year at a $335 million valuation suggests investors think selling picks and shovels to agents is the better trade.

item.title: How Much Did Nuance Labs Raise? Inside the $50M Series A
item.description: Nuance Labs, a Seattle startup building AI that can hold a face-to-face conversation without the awkward pauses, has raised a $50 million Series A led by Lightspeed Venture Partners. NVIDIA and Define Ventures joined as new investors, while Accel and South Park Commons returned from earlier round...
item.content:encoded:
Nuance Labs, a Seattle startup building AI that can hold a face-to-face conversation without the awkward pauses, has raised a $50 million Series A led by Lightspeed Venture Partners. NVIDIA and Define Ventures joined as new investors, while Accel and South Park Commons returned from earlier rounds.


The company was founded by Fangchang Ma, Edward Zhang and Karren Yang, three former Apple researchers who each hold PhDs. Ma serves as co-founder and CEO.


Fixing the Blank Stare


Most AI avatars today work like walkie-talkies. A user speaks, the system waits for silence, processes the request and then replies. The result is a lag that makes digital humans feel stiff, and a tendency to talk over people when they pause mid-thought.


Nuance Labs is building what it calls a foundation model for human conversation and expression. The full-duplex system streams perception and response at the same time, reading words alongside tone, gaze, gesture and timing. That lets the model signal that it is following along while someone is still talking, the way a person nods or reacts in a real exchange.


"The potential for AI and avatars to enhance our lives will never be achieved while they stare at you blankly or keep interrupting you," Ma said.


Where the Money Goes


The company plans to use the new capital to accelerate model development, expand its research team and launch a public research preview of the technology.


Nuance Labs is targeting settings where the quality of a live conversation matters to the outcome. That includes sales and customer service, coaching, professional training, education and environments where people collaborate directly with AI systems.


The round lands as video avatars and voice agents move from demos into real deployments, and as buyers grow less tolerant of interactions that feel robotic. SiliconANGLE framed the raise as an effort to fix the awkwardness that still defines most AI avatars.


Why Lightspeed Doubled Down


Lightspeed led the round as a returning backer, a sign that the firm has seen enough progress since its first check to raise its exposure. Partner Nnamdi Iregbulem described the technology as potential infrastructure rather than a single product.


"We can see this becoming a foundational layer for AI products everywhere, and this is the team to build it," Iregbulem said.


NVIDIA's participation adds a strategic angle. Real-time audiovisual models are compute-heavy, and the chipmaker has been active in backing startups whose workloads run on its hardware.


The Bigger Picture


Large language models have largely solved what AI says. The harder problem now is how it says it. Conversational timing, facial expression and emotional cues are what separate a useful digital coach or service agent from one users abandon after a few seconds.


With a research-heavy founding team, returning investors increasing their commitment and a public preview on the way, Nuance Labs is positioning itself as a model provider for companies that want their AI to feel present in the conversation rather than simply responsive to it.

item.title: What Is Sprive? Inside the $10M Series A for Mortgage Overpayments
item.description: Sprive , the UK mortgage app that turns everyday spending into automatic overpayments, has raised $10 million in a Series A round and has already reached cash flow positivity. The mechanic Sprive's product does something conceptually simple that no bank had bothered to package: users earn cashbac...
item.content:encoded:
Sprive, the UK mortgage app that turns everyday spending into automatic overpayments, has raised $10 million in a Series A round and has already reached cash flow positivity.


The mechanic

Sprive's product does something conceptually simple that no bank had bothered to package: users earn cashback on ordinary purchases, and the app routes that cashback straight at their mortgage principal rather than into a current account. It also monitors the mortgage market and flags refinancing opportunities.


The appeal rests on how mortgage amortization works. An early overpayment reduces the principal on which decades of interest would otherwise compound, so small amounts applied consistently have an outsized effect on total interest paid and term length. Most borrowers understand this in the abstract and never act on it, because doing so requires a deliberate transfer every month. Sprive removes the decision.


The numbers

The company reports 567,000 registered users, £42 billion in supported mortgages, and £26 million in aggregate mortgage balance reductions. 


The commercial figures are the more striking set: revenue up 25x since January 2025, an annual run rate above £18 million, and recently achieved cash flow positivity. A fintech that is cash flow positive before its Series A is raising from a position very few consumer fintechs reach.


That combination also explains the round's structure. No lead investor was named, and the round is a mix of existing and new backers — the shape of a raise the company chose to do rather than needed to do.


The investors

Existing investors Ascension, Channel 4 Ventures and Velocity EIS Technology Fund returned. Active Partners, Wealth Club and Rank Ventures came in new.


The founders

Sprive was founded in 2019 by Jinesh Vohra, who is CEO, and Saad Hashim, both formerly of Goldman Sachs.


Where the money goes

Almost entirely into growth. "With these new funds under our belt... we are now in a strong position to step up our marketing push significantly and accelerate both customer acquisition and revenue growth," Vohra said.

That is the honest version of what this round is for. The product works, the unit economics work, and the constraint is awareness. Most UK homeowners have never heard of the company, and people don't look for mortgage products between renewal dates.


The read

Sprive's position is unusually clean: it makes money, it saves users money in a way that is easy to verify on their own statement, and it sits alongside the mortgage rather than competing with lenders for it. The structural risk is that the mechanic is not hard to copy — a bank or a large cashback platform could bolt overpayment routing onto an existing base far larger than 567,000 users. That's why the entire round is going into marketing, and why the pace of customer acquisition over the next year is the number worth tracking.

item.title: Does Cloud Seeding Work? Rainmaker Raises $100M to Prove It
item.description: Rainmaker , the drone-based cloud seeding company, has raised a $100 million Series B — roughly doubling the $50.3 million it had raised previously, and putting serious institutional money behind a technology that has spent decades stuck between practice and proof. How it works Rainmaker flies cu...
item.content:encoded:
Rainmaker, the drone-based cloud seeding company, has raised a $100 million Series B — roughly doubling the $50.3 million it had raised previously, and putting serious institutional money behind a technology that has spent decades stuck between practice and proof.


How it works

Rainmaker flies custom drones into clouds and releases silver iodide particles, which give water vapor something to condense around and trigger precipitation. Cloud seeding itself is not new — western US states have run programs for decades — but it has always had a measurement problem. If it rains after you seed a cloud, you cannot easily prove it would not have rained anyway.


That is where the drones matter more than the chemistry. Because Rainmaker flies programmed flight patterns, researchers can distinguish precipitation attributable to seeding from what the storm would have produced on its own. Manned aircraft seeding, by contrast, is expensive and imprecise enough that rigorous attribution has been largely impractical.


The traction claim

The company says its programmes have generated 145 million incremental gallons of freshwater. Its August 2026 tests on Alaska's Kenai Peninsula produced 19 million gallons over three hours.


Founder and CEO Augustus Doricko called the Alaska campaign a "significant, precedent-changing shift in our capacity to produce fresh water at scale."


Worth keeping in proportion: 145 million gallons is a meaningful research result and a rounding error against western US water demand. A single mid-sized city gets through that in a day or two. The number that matters is not the total — it is whether the attribution methodology holds up to outside scrutiny.


The investors

NOA VC, Upfront Ventures, DCVC, Lowercarbon Capital and Dream Ventures participated. DCVC and Lowercarbon are both deep-tech and climate specialists with a tolerance for long scientific timelines, which is the correct investor profile for a company whose product is a statistical claim about the weather.


Where the money goes

Much of it goes into science headcount rather than fleet: radar meteorologists, machine learning specialists and aerosol chemists. The company also plans continued collaboration with outside research organizations for validation, and testing of biodegradable seeding agents.

Both of those are as much about legitimacy as capability. Silver iodide is used in small quantities and generally considered environmentally benign at those concentrations, but weather modification attracts public suspicion in a way few technologies do, and "we release chemicals into clouds" is a sentence that does not survive contact with social media intact. Third-party validation and a biodegradable alternative are the answers to a licence-to-operate problem.


The competitive field

Rainmaker is not alone. Recast Systems is testing organic seeding compounds in Texas and New Mexico. The category is being pulled forward by drought severity and by water utilities and agricultural districts running out of conventional options.


The read

Founded in 2023, Rainmaker has raised $150 million total on a thesis that is genuinely unresolved: whether cloud seeding can be made measurable and repeatable enough to sell as water supply rather than as hope. The drones are a real methodological advance on that question. The obstacles are less technical than political — water rights, interstate disputes over who owns precipitation that falls downwind, and a public that did not vote on whether a private company should adjust the weather. A $100 million round buys the company time to produce the evidence. It does not settle the argument.


Source

Fast Company — "Can cloud seeding fight drought? Startup Rainmaker just raised $100 million to find out"

AMPIN Energy Transition has secured a $100 million equity investment from Norfund, the Norwegian government's development finance institution, through its Climate Investment Fund. The round takes AMPIN's total equity raised to roughly $1 billion.


The leverage is the point

Norfund expects the $100 million to mobilize up to $700 million in additional private and debt capital. That ratio, rather than the headline figure, is what a development finance institution is built to produce.

Renewable energy projects in India do not lack commercial lenders so much as they lack the equity layer that makes a project bankable. Patient equity from an institution with a sovereign balance sheet and a climate mandate de-risks the structure enough for commercial debt to follow at reasonable rates. AMPIN has already deployed more than $4 billion in capital on that basis.


What AMPIN has built

The company runs an unusually integrated renewables business: large-scale generation plus backward integration into solar manufacturing.

Its portfolio stands at 6.3 GWp and 5.5 GWh, with 2.5 GWp currently operating across 23 Indian states and union territories. On the manufacturing side it has 1.3 GW of solar cell capacity and 1.9 GW of module capacity. The target is 10 GWp installed by 2030.


The cell and module capacity matters more than it might appear. India has spent several years trying to reduce dependence on imported Chinese solar components, backing domestic manufacturing with content requirements and import duties. A developer that makes its own cells is insulated from both the tariff exposure and the supply shocks that have repeatedly delayed Indian solar projects.


The investor's view

"AMPIN has built an impressive complete renewable energy business... We are pleased to finance AMPIN's next steps," said Bjørnar Baugerud, Norfund EVP.


The word doing the work there is "complete." Norfund is funding vertical integration, not just megawatts — a business that captures margin at manufacturing and generation and is therefore less exposed to the tariff compression that has squeezed pure-play developers as auction prices fell.


Where the money goes

The capital accelerates growth in commercial and industrial and utility-scale renewable projects, expands manufacturing capacity, and funds work further along the energy transition value chain.


The commercial and industrial segment is the interesting emphasis. Utility-scale solar in India has been fiercely competitive on price for years, with margins squeezed by reverse auctions and state distribution companies that are slow to pay. Selling directly to industrial buyers who want cheaper power and have their own decarbonization commitments is better business, with creditworthy offtakers and less exposure to state utility finances.


The read

AMPIN is no longer a venture-stage story — it is an infrastructure company raising structured capital against an operating portfolio, and it follows a $50 million Siemens investment last year. The Norfund check is a vote on Indian renewables generally and on vertical integration specifically. The execution risk is the familiar one in Indian power: land acquisition, grid connectivity queues and distribution-company payment discipline have delayed better-funded projects than this one. Getting from 2.5 GWp operating to 10 GWp by 2030 requires all three to cooperate.

item.title: What Is RESILIENCE? The Docuseries on the Black Tech Funding Gap
item.description: Tech In Black And White has released the first episode of RESILIENCE , a 15-minute documentary that hands the microphone to Black founders, investors and educators and lets them explain the economics of building in tech without a safety net. The Atlanta- and Los Angeles-based production company h...
item.content:encoded:
Tech In Black And White has released the first episode of RESILIENCE, a 15-minute documentary that hands the microphone to Black founders, investors and educators and lets them explain the economics of building in tech without a safety net.


The Atlanta- and Los Angeles-based production company has been documenting Black technologists since May 2018. This episode is its most direct business argument yet: the so-called pipeline problem is, first and last, a capital allocation problem.

A road trip through 30 cities


The film opens on a familiar frustration. "When people meet me, their first thought is not that I'm a computer scientist," one subject says, describing the hoodie-wearing archetype that still stands in for "technologist" in the popular imagination. "You see them in entertainment, but you don't see them in tech."


Rather than argue with the data, the filmmakers went looking past it. "I went out to seek more answers than what the statistics said," the narrator explains, before noting a 30-city search for Black people working in technology. The company is separately in post-production on a pilot called Atlanta Black Tech Mecca.


"The VC doesn't get it because the VC doesn't get you"


The funding chapter is the episode's center of gravity. Dr. Roshawnna Novellus, founder and CEO of the fintech platform EnrichHER, recalls being told to go find a technical co-founder. "My PhD in computer engineering doesn't count as technical," she says. "I worked at IBM Research."


Candace Mitchell Harris, founder of the hair-care recommendation startup Myavana, describes a market that had no frame of reference for her category. "VCs didn't know anything about the hair industry," she says. Her workaround was a circuit of pitch competitions that paid cash: "I raised like over $300,000 just winning pitch competitions," enough to fund the first build of the product. Atlanta angel investor Mike Ross, who appears in the film, was her first check.


Travis and Troy Nunnally, the Georgia Tech-trained brothers known around Atlanta as the Tech Twins, say Black entrepreneurs routinely have to take different routes to capital, without family money behind them. The episode’s blunt summary of the workaround comes from another founder: "Some people may give me $1,000, $100,000, even half a million dollars. That's all good, because I'm going to add it together."


Jay Bailey, president of the H.J. Russell Innovation Center for Entrepreneurs, frames that scarcity as a paradox. "Back against the wall, zero options — that's where entrepreneurs are born," he says, arguing that Black founders would hold a competitive advantage outright "if we had the access, the exposure, the resources, the networks."


Build the pipeline or keep the photo op


South Atlanta instructional coach Andrea Miller delivers the episode's sharpest line on corporate outreach. "Stop giving out free iPads," she says. "My kids need internships that pay." One-hour coding events, she argues, are exposure without transfer: "Gone are the days of what I call the hit-it-and-quit-it interventions."


Her standard is numerical and unsentimental — handoffs from K-12 to undergraduate programs to first jobs that are "intentional and sustained," measured by whether the percentage actually moves. Dr. Jakita Thomas, co-founder of the esports education venture Pharaoh's Conclave, adds the structural read: "The current structures are serving the people who built them very, very well."


Exposure as an asset


Dr. Nashlie Sephus, an applied scientist at Amazon who sold her company to the retailer and now runs the Jackson, Mississippi nonprofit The Bean Path, traces her career to a single summer. A Society of Women Engineers camp at Mississippi State, two hours from home, "changed my life." She went on to a bachelor's at Mississippi State and a PhD at Georgia Tech, often as the only Black woman in the room.


The cost of resilience


The episode closes on the bill that comes due. One founder describes taking a month away from the company after burnout tipped into depression. "Slowing down is a better way to speed up," she says — a maintenance argument for anyone modeling a decade-long company rather than a quick exit.


For readers on the business side, RESILIENCE doubles as a pitch. Tech In Black And White has been open about seeking distribution partners and finishing funds, which makes this episode both a portrait of under-capitalized founders and an artifact of one.


Source


Tech In Black And White — "RESILIENCE Episode 1"

item.title: HEO Raises $25M Series B to Photograph Satellites in Geostationary Orbit
item.description: HEO , the Australian space surveillance company, has raised US$25 million — A$37 million — in a Series B led by Beaten Zone Venture Partners , to extend its satellite inspection business into geostationary orbit. The business: renting other people's cameras HEO photographs satellites and spacecra...
item.content:encoded:
HEO, the Australian space surveillance company, has raised US$25 million — A$37 million — in a Series B led by Beaten Zone Venture Partners, to extend its satellite inspection business into geostationary orbit.


The business: renting other people's cameras

HEO photographs satellites and spacecraft using cameras aboard other satellites, catching them during flybys. Rather than launching a large constellation of its own inspectors, it has access to more than 50 sensors in orbit, eight of which it operates itself.


The capital efficiency of that model is the whole point. Space-based imaging normally means building and launching your own hardware. HEO's approach treats already-orbiting sensors as a distributed network whose spare capacity can be pointed at a target when the geometry lines up.

What customers get is something ground-based tracking cannot provide. A radar station can tell an operator where a satellite is and roughly how it is moving. A photograph taken from a few dozen kilometres away shows whether a solar array actually deployed, whether an antenna is bent, whether the spacecraft is tumbling.


"For commercial players, it allows you to really understand what's wrong with your spacecraft. So a bunch of companies have come to us when something's wrong," said co-founder and CEO William Crowe.


Who is buying

The customer list is the strongest thing in this round: Australia's Department of Defence, Japan's Ministry of Defense and the US National Reconnaissance Office. Those are the hardest procurement processes in the sector, and clearing all three establishes a credibility that is difficult to compete against.


The demand driver is uncomfortable but real. Geostationary orbit holds communications and early-warning satellites that governments consider critical infrastructure, and the number of manoeuvrable objects operating near them has grown. Knowing what is parked next to your satellite has become an operational question rather than an academic one.

"Some of the world's most critical infrastructure is operating tens of thousands of kilometres above Earth, but our ability to see and understand what is happening to it remains limited," Crowe said.


The investors

Beaten Zone Venture Partners led. Australia's National Reconstruction Fund Corporation put in $10 million, joined by Dcode Capital and existing investors Airtree and Salus Ventures.

The NRFC participation marks this as sovereign capability investment as much as venture capital — Australia funding a domestic space asset it would otherwise have to buy from allies.


The GEO expansion

HEO has operated in low-Earth orbit. The Series B funds the move to geostationary orbit through additional sensors, partnerships with satellite operators and software development. The first two launches are scheduled for later in 2026, with regular imaging coverage planned for 2027.

GEO is technically harder. It sits roughly 36,000 kilometres out, and flyby geometry is far less forgiving than in LEO, where orbital planes cross constantly.


The read

HEO spun out of UNSW Founders in 2017 and has reached three national defence customers without the capital those contracts usually require — a function of not owning most of its own hardware. That model is also the dependency: it relies on partner satellites, and partners can change terms. The GEO buildout, with 2027 as the coverage milestone, is where the company finds out whether its approach scales to the orbit its customers care about most.

item.title: Can AI Fix Construction Preconstruction? Wyre AI Raises $5M
item.description: Wyre AI, a construction technology startup using AI to read the mountain of documents that come before a building goes up, has raised $5 million in pre-seed and seed funding led by Ironspring Ventures. WND Ventures, the corporate venture arm of general contractor DPR Construction, and the Virgini...
item.content:encoded:
Wyre AI, a construction technology startup using AI to read the mountain of documents that come before a building goes up, has raised $5 million in pre-seed and seed funding led by Ironspring Ventures.


WND Ventures, the corporate venture arm of general contractor DPR Construction, and the Virginia Innovation Partnership Corporation also invested. Angel backers include Motif CEO and former Autodesk co-CEO Amar Hanspal, Egnyte co-founder Rajesh Ram and Joseph Khoury, co-founder and vice president of preconstruction at MCN Build.


A REPEAT FOUNDER RETURNS TO CONSTRUCTION


Wyre is led by Sunil Dorairajan, who previously founded Pype, a construction document automation company that Autodesk acquired in 2020. Before building software, Dorairajan spent a decade working in preconstruction and operations himself.


That experience shapes his view of the problem. Preconstruction teams still sift through drawings, specifications and contracts by hand, often under tight bid deadlines, and a single missed requirement can turn into a costly change order later.


"The job hasn't fundamentally changed. A few people read thousands of pages under a deadline and hope nothing gets missed," Dorairajan said. "That isn't a staffing problem—it's a technology problem."


TWO PRODUCTS


Wyre offers two tools. Wyre Scopes uses machine learning to analyze project documents and identify the scope of work for each trade. Wyre Check is an AI service that detects clashes and conflicts across documents and shop drawings before they reach the field.


The company has roughly a dozen contractor customers at various stages of deployment, including Rycon Construction, Engineering News-Record reported.


"Whether you're onboarding a new APM or managing concurrent buyouts, it makes the whole team efficient," said Dylan John of Rycon Construction.


WHY THE INVESTORS FIT


Ironspring Ventures focuses on the industrial economy, including construction and supply chain. WND Ventures gives Wyre a direct line to one of the largest general contractors in the country, a meaningful advantage in an industry where adoption often depends on trust and references.


WHY IT MATTERS


Construction remains one of the least digitized major industries, and preconstruction is where many of its costliest mistakes begin. Scope gaps and document conflicts that slip past the bid stage show up later as delays, disputes and budget overruns.


Large language models are well suited to reading dense, text-heavy documents at scale, and a wave of startups is now applying them to construction paperwork. Wyre's edge is a founder who has already sold a company into this exact workflow, and a cap table stacked with people who know how contractors buy software.

item.title: Can Positron AI Take On Nvidia? Inside Its $875M Raise at $5B
item.description: Positron AI, a Reno, Nevada-based chipmaker building hardware for running AI models, has raised $875 million across Series C and Series C-1 financing at a $5 billion post-money valuation. NEA, Atreides Management, Valor Equity Partners, Andra Capital, SemiAnalysis Capital and Netscape co-founder ...
item.content:encoded:
Positron AI, a Reno, Nevada-based chipmaker building hardware for running AI models, has raised $875 million across Series C and Series C-1 financing at a $5 billion post-money valuation.


NEA, Atreides Management, Valor Equity Partners, Andra Capital, SemiAnalysis Capital and Netscape co-founder Jim Clark led the round. DFJ Growth, the Qatar Investment Authority and a long list of others participated, along with strategic investors Hudson River Trading, Cisco Investments and Naver Ventures.


HOW THE ROUND BREAKS DOWN


The financing includes a $375 million Series C priced at a $3.5 billion pre-money valuation, plus a Series C-1 of up to $500 million. Thomas Jermoluk is joining the company's board.


A MEMORY-FIRST BET


Training AI models has made NVIDIA the most valuable chip company in the world, but inference, the work of actually running those models for users, is becoming the larger and faster-growing workload. Inference performance is often limited less by raw compute than by how much memory a chip can access and how quickly.


Positron is designing around that constraint. Its first-generation Atlas system is already running at scale, with more than 50 racks deployed inside Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Other customers include Parasail, Jump Trading and i3d.net.


Its next-generation Asimov chip is set to tape out at the end of 2026 on TSMC's N3P process, with production planned for the second half of 2027. Each Asimov chip will support between 288GB and 2,304GB of memory, using lower-cost LPDDR5X memory, SiliconANGLE noted. A multi-chip system called Titan will combine four to eight Asimov chips.


"Positron is making the boldest memory-first bet in AI hardware," said NEA partner Forest Baskett, pointing to Atlas already running at scale inside Oracle's cloud.


WHERE THE MONEY GOES


Positron will use the funding to tape out Asimov, build a 2-megawatt-plus engineering data center and emulation platform, ramp Titan production and lock in LPDDR5X memory supply commitments.


"Speed matters in this market," said CEO Mitesh Agrawal, adding that lessons from Atlas have been carried directly into Asimov and Titan.


WHY IT MATTERS


An $875 million round makes Positron one of the best-funded challengers in AI chips, a category where hyperscalers and model developers are actively looking for alternatives to NVIDIA to control cost and supply.


The investor mix, spanning venture firms, sovereign wealth, trading firms and networking giant Cisco, signals broad demand for cheaper inference. The real test comes next year, when Asimov has to move from tapeout to production on schedule.

item.title: What Is UrgentIQ? Inside Its $15M Bet on Urgent Care Software
item.description: UrgentIQ, a New York-based software company building electronic medical records for urgent care centers, has raised a $15 million Series A from Five Elms Capital. The growth investment will fund an expansion of the company's AI-native platform into billing, coding and insurance workflows. The dea...
item.content:encoded:
UrgentIQ, a New York-based software company building electronic medical records for urgent care centers, has raised a $15 million Series A from Five Elms Capital. The growth investment will fund an expansion of the company's AI-native platform into billing, coding and insurance workflows.


The deal gives UrgentIQ fresh capital to go after a segment of healthcare that has long been served by general-purpose EMRs designed for hospitals and primary care practices rather than walk-in clinics.


BUILT FOR SPEED


Urgent care runs on volume. Clinics see patients without appointments, move them through quickly and bill a mix of insurers, all with lean staff. UrgentIQ was designed around that reality, combining scheduling, patient intake, clinical documentation, AI-powered coding, revenue cycle management and payment processing in one system.


"Urgent care deserves its own operating system, one designed around speed, intelligence, and automation from the ground up," said Nat Gibbs, UrgentIQ's founder and CEO.


The company serves both independent operators and multi-site urgent care groups nationwide, and says customers report meaningful gains in patient throughput after moving to the platform. Users give the product an average satisfaction rating of 9.7 out of 10.


WHAT THE MONEY BUILDS


UrgentIQ laid out a specific product roadmap for the new capital:


A native billing module that brings more of the revenue cycle in-house rather than relying on outside tools.


Advanced AI diagnosis and coding to speed up documentation and reduce claim errors.


Live insurance verification so front-desk staff can confirm coverage in real time.


An AI checkout agent designed to close out patient visits with less manual work.


Together, those features aim to cut the administrative drag that slows clinics down between the moment a patient walks in and the moment a claim is paid.


WHY FIVE ELMS IS IN


Five Elms Capital, a Kansas City-based growth equity firm focused on B2B software, pointed to the company's traction with operators. "UrgentIQ has built a platform with exceptional operator adoption and product satisfaction," said Joe Onofrio, a partner at the firm.


Vertical software for specialized care settings has become a steady target for investors, especially as AI makes it possible to automate coding and billing tasks that once required dedicated staff. Urgent care, with its high visit counts and thin margins, is a natural fit for that kind of automation.


The urgent care market has expanded as patients look for faster and cheaper alternatives to emergency rooms, and as health systems and private equity-backed groups open new locations. That growth has created more demand for software that can standardize operations across many sites without slowing providers down.


Five Elms focuses on growth-stage B2B software companies, and its investment signals confidence that UrgentIQ can scale from a focused EMR into a full operating platform for the category.


For UrgentIQ, the Series A is a bet that clinics will pay for a system tailored to their workflow rather than adapting one built for someone else.

item.title: Archy Raises $50M Series C to Build AI Back Office for Dentists
item.description: Archy, the San Jose-based dental practice management platform, has raised a $50 million Series C led by JMI Equity. TCV, Entrée Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, CRV and Alven also participated, bringing the company's total funding to $97 million. The startup plans to use the capital to acceler...
item.content:encoded:
Archy, the San Jose-based dental practice management platform, has raised a $50 million Series C led by JMI Equity. TCV, Entrée Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, CRV and Alven also participated, bringing the company's total funding to $97 million.


The startup plans to use the capital to accelerate development of AI agents that automate the administrative work that bogs down dental offices, from insurance claims to clinical notes.


Replacing 20-Year-Old Software


Much of dentistry still runs on legacy, on-premise systems, often literally a server in a closet. Archy was founded in 2021 by CEO Jonathan Rat and CTO Benjamin Kolin to replace that stack with a single cloud platform built for AI from the start.


"Dentists are quickly realizing that slapping a shiny new AI tool onto 20-year-old software doesn't fix their core operational bottlenecks," Rat said in announcing the round.


That argument appears to be landing. Archy now serves more than 1,000 dental practices across 45 states, processes over $300 million in payments annually and supports millions of patients. The company employs about 130 people.


A Suite of Specialized Agents


Rather than one catch-all assistant, Archy has built a set of products aimed at specific pain points in running a practice:


Archy Revenue handles claims filing and collections, one of the most time-consuming jobs for front-office staff.


Archy Scribe generates SOAP notes automatically, cutting documentation time for dentists and hygienists.


Archy Verify checks patient insurance eligibility, while Archy Connect manages patient communications and Archy Insight delivers practice analytics.


Because each tool sits on the same underlying platform, Archy can pass data between scheduling, clinical records and billing without the integrations that bolt-on AI products require.


Why Investors Are Leaning In


Dental care is a large, fragmented market made up largely of independent offices and growing dental service organizations, many of which struggle with staffing shortages at the front desk. Software that reduces manual billing and paperwork translates directly into revenue for practices, which makes the category attractive to growth investors like JMI Equity, a firm known for backing vertical software companies.


The round also reflects a wider trend of AI-native platforms targeting specialized corners of healthcare, where incumbents have been slow to modernize and administrative costs remain stubbornly high.


The funding also arrives as dental groups face pressure from rising labor costs and more complex insurance rules. Every claim that is filed correctly the first time, and every hour a hygienist spends with patients instead of on charting, shows up on a practice's bottom line.


The round pairs lead investor JMI Equity with a deep bench of software backers, including TCV, Bessemer Venture Partners, CRV, Entrée Capital and Alven, giving Archy both capital and operating experience from firms that have scaled vertical SaaS companies before. With 45 states covered, the company's next phase is likely to focus on winning larger multi-location dental groups.


With nearly $100 million raised and a customer base spanning most of the country, Archy's next test is proving that its agents can take on more of the back office without adding friction for patients or staff.

item.title: How Much Did Cornelis Raise? Inside the $205M Bet Against Nvidia
item.description: Cornelis, the AI and high-performance computing networking company spun out of Intel, has raised $205 million to take on Nvidia's grip on data center networking. The round was led by IAG Capital Partners, according to SiliconANGLE . The Wayne, Pennsylvania-based company announced the funding at t...
item.content:encoded:
Cornelis, the AI and high-performance computing networking company spun out of Intel, has raised $205 million to take on Nvidia's grip on data center networking. The round was led by IAG Capital Partners, according to SiliconANGLE.


The Wayne, Pennsylvania-based company announced the funding at the AI Infra Summit alongside a new architecture called Active Compute Fabric, and a collaboration with Qualcomm Technologies on rack-scale AI data center networking.


From Intel Lab to Nvidia Challenger


Cornelis was formed in 2020 when the team behind Intel's Omni-Path interconnect spun out as an independent company. It is now led by CEO Lisa Spelman, a longtime Intel executive who took the top job in 2024.


The pitch is openness. Nvidia sells a tightly integrated stack of GPUs, networking and software. Cornelis is building on open standards, including Ethernet, UALink for scale-up connections inside a rack and Ultra Ethernet for scale-out connections across racks, so data center operators are not locked into a single vendor.


Putting Compute in the Network


The core problem Cornelis is attacking is idle GPU time. In large AI clusters, expensive chips often sit waiting for data to arrive, as TechCrunch noted in its coverage of the round.


Active Compute Fabric embeds programmable compute, including RISC-V cores, directly into the network fabric so it can perform workload-specific operations while data is in transit. Target workloads include KV cache acceleration and mixture-of-experts routing, two bottlenecks in modern AI inference.


"The payload does not arrive the way it left," Chief Marketing Officer Brandon Draeger said, describing how the fabric processes data on the way to its destination. Cornelis says pre-production simulations show up to a 50% reduction in network traffic.


Where the Money Goes


Cornelis will use the capital to scale production of its CN5000 platform, which began shipping in 2025, and its CN6000 line, including an 800-gigabit SuperNIC. The funding also supports the company's expansion into scale-up networking and the rollout of Active Compute Fabric, with a new product generation expected later this year.


The raise dwarfs the $29 million Series B Cornelis announced earlier in its life, a sign of how much investor appetite has grown for the infrastructure layer around AI chips. With hyperscalers and neoclouds spending heavily to squeeze more output from every GPU, networking has become one of the most contested corners of the AI buildout.


Cornelis also argues that better networking changes the economics of AI clusters. If operators can keep GPUs busy instead of waiting on data, they can serve more inference requests or finish training runs sooner on the same hardware, a direct way to improve returns on some of the most expensive equipment in the data center.


The Qualcomm collaboration gives Cornelis a high-profile partner as it moves toward rack-scale systems, where networking, compute and memory are increasingly designed together rather than bought as separate parts.


Whether an open, standards-based approach can pry customers away from Nvidia's integrated systems is the question Cornelis now has $205 million to answer.


Source


TechCrunch — "AI infrastructure company Cornelis raises $205M to chip away at Nvidia's dominance"

item.title: What Does $31M Buy in Warehouse Automation? Vecna Robotics Just Found Out
item.description: Vecna Robotics, the Waltham, Massachusetts-based maker of autonomous warehouse vehicles, has raised $31 million in new funding led by Unless. Existing investors Drive Capital, Tiger Global, Highland Capital Partners and Tectonic Ventures also joined the round. The raise comes as demand grows for ...
item.content:encoded:
Vecna Robotics, the Waltham, Massachusetts-based maker of autonomous warehouse vehicles, has raised $31 million in new funding led by Unless. Existing investors Drive Capital, Tiger Global, Highland Capital Partners and Tectonic Ventures also joined the round.


The raise comes as demand grows for U.S.-built automation that can handle the heavy, repetitive work of moving goods through distribution centers.


Dock to Dock


Vecna builds a lineup of autonomous material handling equipment, including its CaseFlow case-picking system, the CPJ co-bot pallet jack, autonomous forklifts and tuggers. Its Pivotal orchestration software coordinates those machines alongside human workers across a facility.


The company pitches the system as flexible dock-to-dock automation: robots that can take on different tasks as volumes shift, rather than fixed conveyor installations that take months to build and are hard to change.

Demand for CaseFlow


CaseFlow demand has doubled year over year since the product launched in 2025, according to the company.


Logistics provider GEODIS is one customer seeing results. In a case study, the company said picking throughput doubled after deploying the system.


"We're picking twice as much as we did on manual pallet jacks," said Steve Elsbury, senior operations manager at GEODIS. "New pickers typically start at a performance level of 200%."


Where the Money Goes


Vecna plans to use the funding to scale its deployment teams, expand go-to-market efforts, and speed development of new capabilities, including pallet stacking and de-stacking and trailer loading and unloading.


"This investment gives us additional capital to scale what's working today while accelerating capabilities for customers," said CEO Karl Iagnemma.


Iagnemma, who previously co-founded autonomous vehicle company nuTonomy, has steered Vecna toward a narrower set of high-demand warehouse workflows. DC Velocity framed the round around rising demand for robots built in the United States.


Why It Matters


Warehouse operators continue to face labor shortages and high turnover, especially in physically demanding roles like case picking and trailer unloading. That has kept investor interest in warehouse robotics steady even as the broader sector has consolidated.


Trailer loading and unloading in particular remains one of the hardest jobs to automate. If Vecna can extend its platform to that step, it would cover more of the path a pallet travels from the inbound dock to the outbound truck.

item.title: Can AI Learn From Encrypted Data? This Startup, Enigmata, Just Raised $6.5M to Prove It Can
item.description: Enigmata, a Nashville startup building encryption that lets AI work with data it never actually sees, has emerged from stealth with a $6.5 million seed round led by Blockchange Ventures. The company is led by co-founder and CEO Scott Searle. AI on Encrypted Data Companies in healthcare, finance, ...
item.content:encoded:
Enigmata, a Nashville startup building encryption that lets AI work with data it never actually sees, has emerged from stealth with a $6.5 million seed round led by Blockchange Ventures.


The company is led by co-founder and CEO Scott Searle.


AI on Encrypted Data


Companies in healthcare, finance, and government hold some of the most valuable data for training AI, as well as some of the most sensitive. Today that data usually has to be decrypted before a model can learn from it, creating exposure every time it moves.


Enigmata's answer is Enigmata Cipher, a patent-pending cryptographic technology that allows AI systems to train on, search, and analyze encrypted data without exposing the underlying plaintext.


"Every era of computing has forced a choice between using data and protecting it," Searle said. "Enigmata Cipher ends that trade-off."

The Speed Question


Privacy-preserving computation is not new. Techniques such as fully homomorphic encryption have existed for years, but they have struggled to go mainstream because working on encrypted data is typically far slower than working on raw data.


Enigmata says its approach avoids that penalty. In internal benchmarks, models trained on Cipher-protected data matched the accuracy of models trained on raw data and completed training 8% to 10% faster.


Those results have not yet been independently validated, and outside observers have flagged the claim as the one to watch. Remio noted that the speed claim faces a hard test as the technology moves beyond the lab.


Why Blockchange Is In


Blockchange Ventures has historically backed infrastructure in crypto and security, and sees data privacy as the next constraint on AI adoption.


"Privacy is the next great frontier for AI," said Matt Immerso, general partner at Blockchange Ventures, adding that Enigmata built its encryption for that purpose from the ground up.


Why It Matters


As regulators tighten rules on personal data and enterprises grow wary of feeding proprietary information into AI models, the ability to use data without exposing it could unlock datasets that are currently off-limits.


If Enigmata's performance numbers hold up in customer deployments, it would address the main reason encrypted computation has stayed a niche technology. A $6.5 million seed gives the Nashville company room to prove that out with early customers in regulated industries.


Source


PR Newswire — "Enigmata Emerges from Stealth with $6.5 Million to Let AI Learn Without Exposing Sensitive Data"

item.content:encoded:
Piston, a Cupertino, California-based startup replacing the fuel card with a cardless payment network for commercial fleets, has raised a $15 million Series A led by FPV Ventures. Spark Capital and Pear VC also participated, bringing the company's total funding to $22.5 million.


The company was founded by CEO Vikram Sekhon and Shivam Shah.


Taking the Card Out of Fleet Fuel


Trucking and delivery companies have long relied on plastic fuel cards to pay at the pump. Those cards are easy to skim, share or misuse, and fleet operators spend heavily on software that tries to catch fraud after it happens.


Piston removes the card entirely. Its platform uses mobile authorization at the point of sale, approving each purchase for a specific driver and a specific vehicle before fuel is dispensed.


"Fleet fuel fraud is a physical card problem, disguised as a detection issue," Sekhon said. "We removed the card and built a network that authorizes every purchase for a specific driver and vehicle at the point of sale."


Building a Network


Piston says payment volume on its platform grew eight times over the past year, while its merchant network expanded roughly fortyfold. It is now live at more than 2,000 fuel stations across 48 states and reports a 98% customer retention rate.


The company has certified point-of-sale integrations with systems that cover 95% of U.S. merchant fuel sites, a key technical hurdle for any payments company trying to work at the pump.


FPV Ventures partner Nikunj Kothari pointed to the economics of that approach. "Piston moves that money over its own rails, with no card networks or intermediaries in between," he said.


Where the Money Goes


Piston plans to use the Series A to accelerate its national network buildout, continue product development and add senior leadership. The company aims to reach coverage in every U.S. region within 18 months.


Retail Technology Innovation Hub described the round as fuel for building out that U.S. network, which is the core of Piston's pitch to both fleets and fuel merchants.


Why It Matters


Fuel is one of the largest operating expenses for any fleet, and the fleet card market has been dominated for decades by a handful of incumbents that make money on transaction fees. A closed-loop network that cuts out card rails could lower costs for merchants while giving fleet operators tighter control over spending.


The challenge is coverage: drivers need to be able to fill up wherever the route takes them. With 2,000 stations live and integrations reaching most of the country's fuel sites, Piston is betting it can close that gap quickly enough to win fleets away from the plastic card.


Source


FinTech Global — "Piston raises $15m to scale cardless fuel payments"

item.title: Why Is Temporal Worth $12.55 Billion? AI Agent Demand Fuels $550M Raise
item.description: Temporal, the Bellevue, Washington-based company behind an open-source platform that keeps software running through failures, has raised $550 million in a Series E at a $12.55 billion valuation. Lightspeed led the round, with Wellington Management, Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives and ...
item.content:encoded:
Temporal, the Bellevue, Washington-based company behind an open-source platform that keeps software running through failures, has raised $550 million in a Series E at a $12.55 billion valuation. Lightspeed led the round, with Wellington Management, Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives and Tiger Global co-leading.


Returning investors Sequoia Capital, Index Ventures and Madrona joined, along with new backer T. Rowe Price.


The Plumbing Behind AI Agents


Temporal sells what it calls durable execution. In practice, the platform makes sure long-running processes, from payment flows to multi-step AI agent tasks, pick up where they left off when a server crashes, a network drops or an API times out, instead of failing halfway through.


That problem has become far more pressing as companies push AI agents into production. An agent that books travel, reconciles invoices or writes and deploys code may touch dozens of systems in a single task, and every step is a potential point of failure.


"As agents take on more critical work across more systems, every additional step creates another place to fail," said co-founder and CEO Samar Abbas. "In production, that work has to survive those failures and finish reliably."


Growth by the Numbers


The company says its annualized revenue run rate has passed $250 million, growing more than 200% year over year. Its workforce doubled over the past year to 570 employees worldwide.


Temporal counts OpenAI, NVIDIA, Netflix and JPMorgan Chase among its customers, a list that spans the AI labs building agents and the enterprises deploying them.


GeekWire tied the jump in valuation directly to the agentic AI wave, which has turned a niche developer tool into core infrastructure.


Where the Money Goes


Temporal plans to use the funding to accelerate research and development on its platform, expand developer and enterprise go-to-market teams and support its global cloud operations.


Abbas and co-founder and CTO Maxim Fateev first built the underlying technology at Uber, where it powered workflows at massive scale, before spinning it out as an independent company.


"Temporal was built for this problem," Abbas said. "Durable Execution is becoming the standard for reliable applications at scale."


Why It Matters


Much of the investor attention in AI has gone to models and chips. Temporal's round is a reminder that the less visible software layer, the part that makes sure an agent actually finishes the job, is drawing serious capital too.


A $550 million raise with a mix of venture firms and public-market investors such as Wellington and T. Rowe Price also signals that Temporal is building the kind of shareholder base companies typically assemble ahead of an eventual IPO.


Source


Business Wire — "Temporal Raises $550M at a $12.55B Valuation as Demand Surges for Reliable AI Infrastructure"

item.title: Nara Health Raises $14M to Rebuild Employer Health Plans With AI
item.description: Nara Health, a Chicago startup rebuilding how employers administer self-insured health plans, has raised $14 million across pre-seed and seed rounds led by Khosla Ventures. Long Journey Ventures, Superior Studios and a group of strategic angel investors also participated. The company operates as ...
item.content:encoded:
Nara Health, a Chicago startup rebuilding how employers administer self-insured health plans, has raised $14 million across pre-seed and seed rounds led by Khosla Ventures. Long Journey Ventures, Superior Studios and a group of strategic angel investors also participated.


The company operates as an AI-native third-party administrator, or TPA, the behind-the-scenes layer that handles claims, benefits and member support for employers that fund their own health coverage.


Rebuilding the TPA


Self-insured employers typically stitch together several vendors to run a health plan: one for claims, another for navigation, another for care management. Nara Health combines benefits administration, claims processing, member navigation and care orchestration in a single platform.


The company pairs that software with alternative plan designs, including direct provider contracting, reference-based pricing, cash-pay pricing and Direct Primary Care. Agentic AI then coordinates care for members inside those plans.


"By bringing benefits administration, claims processing, care orchestration, and member support into a single intelligent platform, Nara Health helps employers lower healthcare costs while making it dramatically easier for employees to access and use their benefits," said co-founder and CEO Sidhartha Sinha.


Early Traction


Nara Health already covers more than 25,000 lives and has processed over $600 million in aggregate medical claims. The company says member support questions are answered in about five seconds and prior authorizations are handled the same day, compared with the three to five business days common across the industry.


Employers on the platform have cut year-over-year healthcare spend by 15% to 50%, according to the company. In one case study, Advanced Medical Pricing Solutions reported a 55% reduction in benefits costs.


A Founder Built for the Problem


Sinha has spent his career on the delivery side of healthcare, designing hospitals and care models and building AI products for health systems and insurers. That background shapes a pitch focused as much on access as on cost.


"Our care has been limited by our coverage — that should never be the case," Sinha said.


Why It Matters


Employer health costs keep climbing, and more mid-sized companies are moving to self-funded plans to gain control over spending. That shift has created an opening for administrators that can do more than process paperwork.


Khosla Ventures has made a series of bets on AI reshaping healthcare operations, and Nara Health fits that thesis: a back-office function that has changed little in decades, now rebuilt around automation. MedCity News also covered the raise as a bet on the third-party administration model.


For employers weighing a switch, the numbers Nara Health is putting forward, same-day authorizations and double-digit savings, are the kind that tend to get a CFO's attention.


Source


Business Wire — "Nara Health Raises $14M to Reinvent Health Insurance Through AI Benefits Administration and Alternative Health Plans"

item.title: What Is FAZE Security? The AI Red Teaming Startup With a $6M Seed
item.description: FAZE Security has emerged from stealth with $6 million in seed funding led by New Era Capital Partners, with participation from Lockstep VC. The New York-based cybersecurity company is building an offensive security orchestration platform powered by autonomous AI agents. Unlike most seed-stage st...
item.content:encoded:
FAZE Security has emerged from stealth with $6 million in seed funding led by New Era Capital Partners, with participation from Lockstep VC. The New York-based cybersecurity company is building an offensive security orchestration platform powered by autonomous AI agents.


Unlike most seed-stage startups, FAZE is not launching with a prototype. The company says it already works with about 50 enterprise customers, including several Fortune 500 companies, and has grown annual recurring revenue roughly 20X over the past 18 months.


ATTACKING LIKE A HACKER


FAZE's platform runs what it describes as autonomous agentic red teaming. Its AI agents are trained on proprietary attack data gathered from white-hat hackers, and they continuously probe web applications, APIs and cloud environments the way a real attacker would.


The key distinction is proof. Many security tools generate long lists of theoretical risks and severity scores, leaving teams to guess which ones matter. FAZE's agents attempt to simulate actual exploits, showing which weaknesses can be used to break in and which are noise.


That approach targets one of the biggest pain points in enterprise security: alert fatigue. Security teams are overwhelmed with findings and short on the staff needed to validate them, and traditional penetration tests happen only periodically while applications change constantly.


A REBRAND AND A LAUNCH


The company previously operated under the name CYTRIX before stepping out publicly as FAZE Security alongside the funding announcement, according to The SaaS News.


Its lead investor, New Era Capital Partners, recently closed a $120 million fund aimed at Israeli-founded startups, per CTech, adding FAZE to a portfolio focused on companies building for global markets.


WHAT COMES NEXT


FAZE plans to use the seed capital to support continued growth and expand the capabilities of its offensive security orchestration platform as it moves from stealth into a more visible go-to-market push.


The timing fits a broader shift in the industry. As attackers adopt AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster, defenders are turning to AI agents that can test systems continuously instead of waiting for the next scheduled audit. A wave of startups is now competing to automate the work of human red teams and penetration testers.


For buyers, the promise is fewer false alarms and faster fixes. When a platform can demonstrate that a vulnerability is exploitable, security and engineering teams have a clearer case for prioritizing it, and less time is wasted debating findings that pose little real risk.


Continuous testing also matters as companies ship code more often. An application that passed last quarter's penetration test may look very different after weeks of new releases, integrations and cloud configuration changes, and every one of those changes can open a new path for attackers that a point-in-time assessment would miss.


With revenue traction already in hand and Fortune 500 logos on its customer list, FAZE enters that race with more proof points than most companies at the seed stage.


SOURCE


PR Newswire — "FAZE Security emerged from stealth today with 50 enterprise customers"

item.title: HiBob Raises $166M at $3.2B Valuation: Investors & Revenue
item.description: HiBob, the HR platform behind Bob, has raised $166 million in a round led by Salesforce with participation from Farallon Capital Management. The investment values the company at $3.2 billion, according to SiliconANGLE , up from the $2.7 billion mark it reached when it raised $150 million in 2023....
item.content:encoded:
HiBob, the HR platform behind Bob, has raised $166 million in a round led by Salesforce with participation from Farallon Capital Management. The investment values the company at $3.2 billion, according to SiliconANGLE, up from the $2.7 billion mark it reached when it raised $150 million in 2023.


The raise comes as HiBob's annualized revenue has climbed past $400 million. The company, co-founded in 2015 by CEO Ronni Zehavi, operates out of New York and London and serves more than 5,500 organizations across 170-plus countries.


Salesforce's lead role and the $3.2 billion price were also reported by CTech. The new valuation represents roughly a $500 million step-up from 2023, a period in which HiBob's revenue base has continued to grow as late-stage software valuations reset across the market.


Why Salesforce Is Writing the Check


The deal is as strategic as it is financial. Salesforce and its Slack unit have been deepening integrations with HiBob, and both sides frame the investment around what they call "trusted workforce context," the org charts, roles, skills and employee data that AI tools need to be useful inside a company.


Joe Teplow, who oversees strategy for Slack and Salesforce's venture efforts, pointed to HiBob's "deep understanding of how organizations operate." Slack CMO Ryan Gavin added that workforce context makes AI "more relevant to the teams using it."


Zehavi framed the moment in bigger terms. "The biggest mistake companies can make is to think AI is primarily a technology story," he said. "It is an organizational and managerial revolution."


Inside the Platform


Bob started as a core HR system and has grown into a broader people platform. It centralizes employee records and workforce management, and includes Bob Skills, a database that maps the expertise employees already have inside a company.


On the hiring side, HiBob uses AI to generate job descriptions, distribute listings to more than 2,300 job boards, summarize incoming CVs and manage employee referrals and branded careers pages. A workforce planning tool lets HR teams simulate headcount growth before they commit to it.


The platform also includes an employee portal for company updates and tasks, a learning management system that pulls in third-party courses, and an MCP server that lets companies sync HR data into outside automation and AI tools. AI-driven course recommendations are on the roadmap.


What Comes Next


HiBob says the capital will back its push toward "organizational intelligence," using the people data it already holds to power AI experiences across collaboration, CRM, finance and operations software. Expect Slack to be a central surface for that work, with more conversational, employee-facing features built around HiBob's data.


Despite the revenue scale and a fresh unicorn-plus valuation, company leadership said an IPO is not currently in the plans. For now, HiBob is betting that owning the system of record for people will matter more, not less, as enterprises roll AI agents into daily work, and that Salesforce is the right partner to prove it.


The round lands during a busy stretch for HR tech funding, as investors look for software companies whose proprietary data can give AI products an edge over general-purpose models.
